utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. I declare this hearing open. Madam Registrar, please call the case for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is the case number IT-01-42-A, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to know whether Mr. Strugar is in a position to hear and to follow the proceedings in a language he understands? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to ask for the appearances of the parties starting with Mr. Strugar's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Pavle Strugar, before the Appeals Chamber today, counsel Goran Rodic from Podgorica and counsel Vladimir Petrovic from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me now turn to the office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution, together with Michelle Jarvis, Laurel Baig, Xavier Tracol, and our case manager, Sebastian van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Brady. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the parties's submissions related to the appeals filed by Mr. Strugar and by the OTP against the Trial Chamber's judgement. Before I give the floor to the parties, I am going to briefly summarise the grounds of appeal pending before the Appeals Chamber and I will also outline the way we will proceed today. In its judgement rendered on the 31st of January, 2005, the Trial Chamber II, made up of Judge Parker presiding, Judge Thelin and Judge Van den Wyngaert, sentenced Pavle Strugar to a single sentence of eight years of imprisonment for the counts he was found guilty of. Namely, count 3, attacks on civilians pursuant to Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute; count 6, destruction or wilful damage to cultural property pursuant to Articles 3(d) and 7(3) of the Statute. Both parties appealed the trial judgement. At the request of the parties, the Appeals Chamber accepted the withdrawal of these appeals on the 20th of September, 2006, and then the appeals proceedings were reopened on the 7th of June, 2007. Under his first and third grounds of appeal, Strugar submits that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact. Firstly, he contends that several findings contained in the judgements are erroneous with respect to JNA combat operations in the Dubrovnik area in October and November 1991. Under the same sub-ground of appeal, he submits that the Trial Chamber erroneously found that the mental element required to establish his superior responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute had been satisfied. Secondly, Mr. Strugar alleges that the Trial Chamber committed an error in relation to the events of the 3rd and 5th of December, 1991, with respect to his responsibility in the negotiations with Croatian ministers and in the planning of the attack against Srdj. Thirdly, Strugar maintains that the Trial Chamber committed errors related to the events of the 6th of December, 1991. Fourthly, Strugar submits that the Trial Chamber committed an error in relation to his failure to prevent crimes and, in particular, in respect to the command structure of the 2nd Operational Group, his material ability to prevent crimes, his measures to prevent or stop the shelling of the Old Town, and finally, the cease-fire order. As a fifth point, Strugar alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's findings regarding his material ability to punish, his failure to take measures after the events of the 6th of December, 1991, and the promotions and decorations awarded to individuals involved in these events. Under his second ground of appeal, Strugar submits, first of all, that the Trial Chamber erroneously concluded that the legal requirement of a superior subordinate relationship was established on the facts of this case. Under the second sub-ground of this ground of appeal, Strugar submits that the Trial Chamber erred in its conclusions in relation to the mens rea for the following crimes: Attack on civilians and destruction or wilful damage to cultural property. For example, in its findings related to indirect intent. Under his fourth ground of appeal related to sentencing, Strugar submits that the Trial Chamber committed an error in its comparison of his sentence and that of Miodrag Jokic in failing to assign due weight to his apologies and in failing to give sufficient weight to some mitigating circumstances. Finally, as part of his fifth and last ground of appeal, Strugar raises issues related to his fitness to stand trial in the first place. Mr. Strugar therefore requests the Appeals Chamber to acquit him on all charges against him or alternatively to order a new trial or to significantly reduce his sentence. He also requests the Appeals Chamber to terminate judicial proceedings in his case on the grounds that he was and still is not fit to stand trial. The Prosecution requests that the totality of Strugar's grounds of appeal be dismissed. As mentioned earlier, the Prosecution has also appealed against the trial judgement. Under its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law in its application of the test related to mens rea required under Article 7(3) of the Statute in holding that prior to the attack on Srdj launched in the early hours of the 6th of December, 1991, Strugar did not know or have any reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit an offence. Alternatively, the Prosecution submits that even if the Trial Chamber's interpretation of the law is correct, the Trial Chamber, nonetheless, erred in fact in finding that it had not been established that prior to the attack on Srdj, Strugar had reasonable grounds to suspect that his subordinates were about to commit an offence. Under his second ground of appeal, the Prosecutor submits that the Trial Chamber committed an error in the application of the law on cumulative convictions for grounds -- for counts 4, devastation not justified by military necessity. Count 5, unlawful attacks on civilian objects. And Count 6, destruction or wilful damage to cultural property. Finally, under its third and last ground of appeal related to sentencing, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in its comparison of Mr. Strugar's sentence and Miodrag Jokic's sentence and in holding that the apologies of Mr. Strugar constitute a mitigating circumstance. The Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to reverse the Trial Chamber's finding that Mr. Strugar did not have the obligation to prevent the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik prior to the beginning of the attack against Srdj and to adjust the sentence accordingly. Furthermore, the Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to enter convictions under Counts 4 and 5 of the indictment and that Mr. Strugar's sentence be increased. During today's hearing, the parties may decide to put forth their grounds and sub-grounds of appeal in the order they see fit. However, I would like to remind the parties that they have been invited to address a number of issues outlined in the memorandum sent to them on the 20th of March, 2008. I'm not going to repeat what was mentioned in that memo. I'm now going to record what standards are applicable to errors of fact or errors of law raised on appeal. Appeals against judgement do not constitute de novo trials. The parties cannot merely repeat the arguments they have already made in a trial. Under Article 25 of the Statute, the role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting legal errors that invalidate a decision and factual errors that result in a miscarriage of justice. As a result, any party alleging a error of law must present arguments in support of its claim and explain how the error invalidates the decision. As for factual errors, it is well-established in the jurisprudence that the Appeals Chamber will not likely disturb findings of fact by a Trial Chamber. The Appeals Chamber will only do so when it has been established that no reasonable trier of facts could have reached the same conclusion or when the conclusion is wholly erroneous. Furthermore, the Appeals Chamber may dismiss summarily without reviewing them on the merits the arguments submitted by a party that have no chance to lead to a reversal or a change of the impugned decision. Appealing parties furthermore need and must provide specific references to all the elements supporting their case on appeal. Furthermore, it cannot be expected of the Appeals Chamber to review in detail the parties' submissions if such submissions are obscure, contradictory or vague or if they suffer from other formal and obvious deficiencies. Finally, the Appeals Chamber has an inherent discretion to determine which of these submissions merit a reasoned opinion in writing and will therefore dismiss arguments which are evidently unfounded without providing a detailed reasoning in writing. In this hearing, we'll proceed pursuant to the Scheduling Order of 29th of January, 2008. The Defence will start with its submissions for an hour and a half. We'll then have a 20-minute break. The Prosecution will start responding during an hour. We'll have a one-hour break, and the Defence will have 30 minutes to reply. Following that, the Prosecution will make its own submissions for an hour and a half, and we'll have a 20-minute break in the middle of this presentation. The Defence will have one hour to respond to the Prosecution. We'll have a last break of 20 minutes and then the Prosecution will have 30 minutes to reply. Finally, Mr. Strugar will be invited to take the floor, if he wishes to do so, for a short statement that should not be longer than 15 minutes. The Appeals Chamber would find it extremely useful if the parties could make their submissions in a clear, organised and concise fashion. At any time, the Judges may interrupt the parties to ask for clarification or put questions. Obviously, the parties do not have to use all the time given to them. If there aren't any questions about the way we are going to proceed today, I am now going to invite the Defence to start with its submissions on appeal. Fine. The Defence has the floor. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Pavle Strugar has launched an appeal against the judgement of the Trial Chamber dated the 31st of January, 2005. In our appeal, we gave a thorough presentation of the reasons for which we believe that the Trial Chamber's judgement was reached after errors were committed, errors of law and errors of fact resulting in a miscarriage of justice. The Defence fully accepts the standard of review for judgements reached by Trial Chambers in terms of errors of law and errors of fact. These criteria are well-established in the jurisprudence of this International Tribunal. In our appellate brief, we pointed out how certain errors were made that have repercussions on the miscarriage of justice. The Defence pointed out errors that were made that in terms of their nature and gravity require the intervention of the Appeals Chamber by quashing the original judgement or revising or reversing certain conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber. The Defence has grouped the areas that it believes the Trial Chamber to have committed in -- as five grounds with a number of sub-grounds. The Defence abides by what is stated in its appellate brief. The Defence will use this opportunity to underline certain errors made by the Trial Chamber. The Defence particularly wishes to point out these errors in order to have them clarified. Likewise, the Defence will do everything within its power to avoid repetition of what has already been said and written to the greatest possible extent and thereby contribute to a speedy, efficient, and effective hearing. The Defence believes that there is no evidence suggesting that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj. One of the key errors made by the Trial Chamber was the finding that Pavle Strugar had ordered an attack on Srdj. The Trial Chamber found that Strugar issued that order on the 5th of December, 1991. This finding was reached based on the evidence of Prosecution witness, Colm Doyle. There is one key sentence in Doyle's evidence, I quote: "And the interpreter informed me that the General had been quite angry because of what was termed to me as paramilitaries on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had attacked some of his troops. The troops that were under General Strugar's command. This was something he would not tolerate. And he responded by firing on the city of Dubrovnik." The transcript page is 1716. The Defence also wishes to point out in relation to the Strugar-Doyle meeting one thing that is particularly important. Strugar and Doyle communicated through an interpreter. Objectively speaking, we must raise the following issue: Was everything interpreted in its entirety? Did Strugar actually use the words in the same way as they were rendered to Colm Doyle. When Doyle remembers that particular conversation he claims he cannot remember the exact words used by Strugar or those conveyed by the interpreter, meaning there was no direct communication. Colm Doyle took no notes and wrote down no details of that meeting. The Defence would particularly like to point out that Doyle does not say a single word about Srdj [Realtime transcript read in error "search"], not a single word about the attack on Srdj. No mention at all -- for the sake of the transcript, it reads search, the English word search as opposed to B/C/S Srdj which is the name of the hill, that at 0320, Srdj is a place name. This is a hill above Dubrovnik. I will repeat this. The Defence would particularly like to point out that Doyle does not say a single word about Srdj, not a single word about the attack on Srdj. No mention at all of Croatia's paramilitary units. The Trial Chamber, heard the following words: "Opened fire on the city of Dubrovnik," and that was a quote. The interpretation provided by the Trial Chamber is quite random. It draws the inference based on those words that Strugar issued an order to attack Srdj. Moreover, the Trial Chamber finds these words to be an unequivocal admission on the part of General Strugar that he issued an order to attack Srdj. This is a sentence recorded by Mr. Doyle to the Trial Chamber, however, based on this, all that any reasonable trier of fact could find is that Strugar was angry that paramilitary units in Bosnia and Herzegovina had attacked JNA units under Strugar's command. Another possible inference would be that as a response to those attacks, fire was opened on Dubrovnik. Nevertheless, one thing that is impossible to find based on this evidence is that Strugar actually issued an order to attack Srdj on the 5th of December, 1991. Witness Doyle talks about Bosnia alone, and about the attack carried out by paramilitary units in that republic. Doyle is unambiguous about the fact that Strugar never specified the paramilitary units in question. Doyle does not even utter the word "Srdj." Doyle probably doesn't even know where Srdj is. Witness Doyle knows nothing about any order allegedly issued by Strugar to open fire. Doyle knows nothing about what the potential targets of such an attack might be. Strugar never specified any order given, nor indeed does Doyle address this. Doyle's impression is that Strugar talks about opening fire in an entirely generic way. Doyle unequivocally states this in his evidence before the Trial Chamber. Doyle also confirms that in actual fact, he no longer even remembers the exact words spoken by Strugar. Doyle's evidence is full of impressions and assumptions. Doyle provides assumptions about Strugar's moods and the reasons for those moods or dispositions. He provides assumptions about where exactly Strugar's units had been attacked. He provides assumptions about what sort of an order Strugar had issued in relation to Dubrovnik itself. However, all Colonel Doyle provided are fragments of vague memories based on which the Trial Chamber puts together an entire construct of erroneous and impossible findings. Doyle's evidence does not even provide a decent basis for one of the most far-reaching findings in the judgement itself. This is a finding on which the responsibility of my client was found to be based. The Trial Chamber finds, based on Doyle's evidence, that Strugar must have ordered the attack simply because the attack occurred. We believe this finding by the Trial Chamber to be untenable. The fact that the attack eventually occurred says nothing about the circumstances of the attack on Srdj, nor indeed does it tell us anything about the role of Pavle Strugar. The attack on Dubrovnik and the attack on Srdj are not the same thing nor can they ever be. One thing that remains unclear is this: The peak of that hill has an altitude of 400 metres above sea level and above Dubrovnik, there is nothing there apart from the repeater and the -- and the final stop of a cable car from Dubrovnik. Yet the Trial Chamber sees this as being identical to the city of Dubrovnik itself simply because when Doyle says Srdj, this is taken by the Trial Chamber to mean the same as Dubrovnik. There is no evidence at all that was presented during trial to suggest that the words Dubrovnik and Srdj mean the same thing and that when Srdj is used, Dubrovnik is what is meant. Nothing at all to suggest that. If we look at the findings of the Trial Chamber, it would seem that their interpretation was that Strugar's aim was to conceal the real intention behind the attack that he allegedly issued, the taking of the facilities in Srdj and that is why Strugar never tells him that he was attacking Srdj, a hill above the town, but rather spoke of the city of Dubrovnik as the target of the attack which was potentially beyond the pale. Based upon what Strugar did not say, the finding is reached about an attack on a legitimate military target which is a target that allegedly Strugar kept silent about. All this is interpreted by the Trial Chamber as a direct admission by Strugar. The Chamber even goes as far as to establish that Strugar was nervous during the meeting. It was Strugar's apparent mood that led them to establish that his dissatisfaction was directly linked to the progress of an action that he had allegedly ordered. It is particularly difficult to believe that Strugar gave this admission as the Trial Chamber interprets the conversation between Strugar and Doyle to a military observer, an officer of the Irish army whom he had never before set eyes on. Equally noteworthy is the moment when allegedly Strugar made this admission. The alleged admission was made at a moment in relation to which the Trial Chamber finds that Strugar had already known about the fact that the Old Town had been targeted and hit. By this time, the Trial Chamber finds that he had been summoned to Belgrade by the Defence minister General Kadijevic and the chief of general staff of the JNA. He was summoned to discuss developments around Dubrovnik that morning. The Trial Chamber goes on to establish that Strugar, by this time, must have been fully aware of the extent of the problem. In the interpretation of the Trial Chamber, this was an admission that Strugar made at the time under the circumstances described. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the Trial Chamber finds that at 11.15 on the 6th of December, Strugar allegedly ordered a cease-fire. Following that order, the intensity of shelling in Dubrovnik diminished. Therefore, bearing in mind the aforementioned, a mere 45 minutes before his meeting with Doyle, Strugar had ordered a cease-fire. The Chamber finds that the meeting with Doyle took place at about 1200 hours. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber believes that regardless of the fact that a cease-fire had been ordered, Strugar was still using Doyle's presence to inform him that an attack was in progress as they spoke which he had personally ordered. Another thing that is noteworthy is the fact that Strugar "admits" to an Irish officer that he had ordered an attack yet at the same time, the Trial Chamber finds that Strugar was allegedly concocting a plan with Admiral Jokic for a cover-up of everything that had occurred and a plan of how to shift responsibility to Captain Kovacevic. Admiral Jokic and Strugar that afternoon, the 6th of December, 1991, are on their way to see Federal Minister Kadijevic, the supreme military leader of the country. Admiral Jokic now tells him that the attack on Srdj was a wanton attack launched by Captain Kovacevic. How could Strugar possibly have admitted to an officer of the Irish army that he had ordered an attack while at the same time he was trying to conceal the truth on this alleged attack from the Defence Minister of Yugoslavia and the Chief of Staff of the JNA? The Trial Chamber reached a conclusion that is simply not credible. Strugar makes an admission to this Irish military officer. He admits that he ordered the attack, yet he does his best to conceal this same fact from the top-most leadership of the JNA. How credible is it that Strugar would choose to speak in confidence to a high-ranking member of the European monitoring mission in Yugoslavia who also happened to be in daily contact with high-ranking JNA officers? This is obvious based on a number of different witnesses and testimonies in this case. It is quite certain that they would have conveyed to him what they found out from Strugar through these contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I simply ask the counsel to be so kind when he makes references to something that the Trial Chamber did, could he refer to the specific paragraphs in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those are paragraphs in the Trial Chamber's judgement beginning with 164 through 169. Is this answer to your satisfaction, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber does not invoke any other evidence whatsoever nor does it provide answers to a whole series of questions that are thereby opened only on the basis of the finding that allegedly Strugar ordered an attack on the Old Town. Why did Strugar have to order this attack precisely on the 5th of December? To whom did he issue this order? Who received the order to attack? How did Strugar pass this order on? What was contained in the order to attack, allegedly issued by Strugar? What were the targets of attack? At what time was the attack to be committed? With what resources? Which units were to be involved? On what axis? We do not know whether in this alleged order to attack Srdj, Strugar similarly to his prior conduct and the current and valid order on the cease-fire and prohibition of shelling of the Old Town of the 11th of November, 1991, this time too he ordered that the Old Town must not be shelled. All these are questions that the Trial Chamber does not answer in its judgement. The Trial Chamber attempts to corroborate its finding on the alleged order by Strugar by the assertion that it is logical that Strugar ordered the attack to capture Srdj because it is in keeping with the military realities of the JNA. First and foremost, the Chamber has no evidence about military realities of the JNA and what they are. It relies solely on conjecture. If it is assumed that there is a relationship of subordination between the 9th Military Naval Sector and Commander Jokic and the 2nd Operations Group commanded by Strugar, then everything undertaken by the 9th Military Naval Sector must be in keeping with orders from the 2nd Operations Group. If we accept that this is the logic lying in the foundations of the JNA, and that this is the so-called military reality of the JNA, and if this logic were to be accepted unconditionally and automatically as the Trial Chamber accepts it, then the only possible conclusion would be that the attack on Srdj was ordered by the Minister for Defence and the JNA General Staff. Because if it is inconceivable, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, that a unit at corps level launches an action without an order from the unit at army level to which it belongs, then it is equally inconceivable that a strategic group at the level of army implements an action without orders from the General Staff of the JNA and the Minister of Defence personally. What we have here is an action by two armed task forces with less than 40 men who were supposed to capture a feature by surprise attack. The Defence emphasises that the military realities of the JNA call for an analysis of this specific situation. There is nothing automatic about it. There is only an analysis to be made of the various roles of protagonists of the events of the 6th of December, 1991. Concluding that Strugar ordered something because that would be logical is not a finding beyond any reasonable doubt. The Defence asserts that not a single reasonable trier of fact could make a finding made by this Trial Chamber regarding the order to attack Srdj. It is of decisive importance for establishing the command responsibility of Strugar for the actions of his subordinates to establish whether Strugar ordered this attack. It is on this fact that the finding whether Strugar is one of the people responsible for the events of the 6th of December, 1991, depends. Without this fact, any person, and every person in the chain of command would be responsible for every action perpetrated within the military structure. The Defence concludes that the finding that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj that should have been launched on the 6th of December, 1991, is impossible. Equally impossible is the finding that Strugar ordered it on the 5th December. This is also confirmed by erroneous findings of the Trial Chamber regarding important facts contained in the evidence of Admiral Jokic and the entire approach of the Trial Chamber to this evidence. First of all, there are numerous contradictions in the testimony of Jokic that are most frequently manifested in the fact that regarding one event or one fact, he has several versions. For instance, his presence at the meeting at the forward command post of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kupari on the 5th of December, 1991. It is typical that in several places in the judgement, the Trial Chamber qualifies Jokic's testimony as, I quote: "Certain aspects of Jokic's testimony can be qualified as less than satisfactory." Further on: "It is difficult to accept all the claims made by Jokic on his actions that morning." Further on: "The Trial Chamber does not reject Jokic's explanation out of hand but believes it is not credible." Next quotation, "The Federal Secretariat for National Defence was informed briefly by Jokic about the damage and actions of the 6th December in a way that was rather inconsistent with facts." Next quotation, "Jokic's explanation why he failed to take disciplinary measures is not believable, is not persuasive." Another quotation, "The Trial Chamber has the reservations regarding what was discussed exactly when Jokic made his report." These are only some of the qualifications made by the Trial Chamber of Jokic's testimony indicating that the Trial Chamber did not believe Jokic when he testified about important facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could you give us a reference each time you quote something? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These quotations are in the following paragraphs of the judgement: 152, 153, 97, 174 -- 174 and 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I was saying, these were only some of the qualifications of Jokic's testimony made by the Trial Chamber indicating that the Trial Chamber did not believe Jokic when he was testifying about important facts. However, there was not a single case when the Trial Chamber said that it was untruthful testimony or that Jokic had vested interests as a witness, something that the Trial Chamber did in other cases. For instance, for the reasons explained earlier, in relation to the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic, commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade of the 9th Military Naval Sector who says emphatically that General Jokic was present at the meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December when Captain Kovacevic made his proposal to attack Srdj, the Trial Chamber states, I quote: "The Trial Chamber does not accept that this testimony is truthful." Paragraph 98 in the judgement. No reasons are stated why this testimony was found to be untruthful. Objectively, this would be difficult to explain since the Trial Chamber admitted into evidence the written report that Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic made to the superior commander on the 6th of December referring, again, to Jokic's presence at the meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December. But in paragraph 98 -- 88 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber states: "The issue whether Jokic was at the meeting in Kupari is not a key issue although it is relevant, this issue has a relevance -- although it has relevance, it is not determinative of the Chamber's decision." Also in paragraph 339 of the judgement, I quote: "In the finding of the Trial Chamber, evidence indicates that the detailed planning for the implementation of this order," and the order to attack Srdj was meant, "the accused left it to the 9th Military Naval Sector which had geographical responsibility for Dubrovnik and its surrounds. There are unresolved issues about the role of the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector; however, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, actively involved were Chief of Staff Warship-Captain Zec and other staff officers were active in the planning and execution of the order both on the 5th and 6th December, 1991." The Defence believes this finding of the Trial Chamber is erroneous when the Trial Chamber holds that Jokic's presence at the meeting in Kupari on the 5th December is not determinative for the Trial Chamber's decision. As the Defence emphasised in the appeal, Strugar denies that he ordered the attack on Srdj and Jokic's presence at the meeting in Kupari would confirm that he both -- that he participated both in the planning and the implementation of the attack on Srdj. When the Trial Chamber elaborates on military realities in the JNA in this context, it is necessary to emphasise the following findings of fact made by the Trial Chamber, namely that Jokic's Chief of Staff, Frigate Captain Zec, participated in the planning of the attack on Srdj, paragraph 87 and 88. That he personally brought the equipment for the attack, paragraph 88. That Zec was presented at Zarkovica throughout the day, meaning the 6th of December, 1991. Paragraph 126. That not even when Zec returned to Zarkovica after a 30-minute meeting with Jokic in saftat [phoen] did the attack on Srdj cease. Witness Kurdulija. That Zec, upon returning to Zarkovica looks for engineers with explosives to complete the action, Exhibit D96, 1330 hours. All that time, Jokic avoids informing Strugar of these events believing that, as he says, the latter has more important things to do. Everything seems to indicate that the attack was ordered and planned within the 9th Military Naval Sector without a single piece of evidence about the involvement of General Strugar in the ordering and execution of that attack. The Trial Chamber does not lend credence even to the second version presented by Jokic concerning the attack on Srdj; namely, that the planning and ordering of this action was deliberately concealed from him, paragraph 437 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber states the following reason: "If it had been that way, the conduct of his Chief of Staff Frigate Captain Zec would have called for the most severe disciplinary action, their personal and professional relationship would have been shattered, yet no action was taken and both the admiral and Warship-Captain Zec continued in their previous roles as commander and Chief of Staff of the 9th Military Naval District." It is curious, thus, nothing was held back from Jokic and yet the Trial Chamber erroneously holds that it is not determinative for the Trial Chamber's decision in this case and that the question of Jokic's presence at the meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December, 1991, remains open. After Jokic's investigation on the 6th of December, or rather, what had happened on the 6th of December, the only consequence is that Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic was urgently replaced, that is the witness who testified that Jokic attended the meeting on the 5th of December. As for Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic, the Trial Chamber established that he could not have taken action against the old city and that is also what Admiral Jokic knows. Bearing in mind the aforementioned, when one knows that the Prosecution withdrew the charges Warship-Captain Zec in 2003, also that Captain Kovacevic was declared incompetent to stand trial, unfit for trial, and that the judgement is based on the erroneous finding of the Trial Chamber that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj, the Defence therefore believes that it is impossible to find that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj that was supposed to be carried out on the 6th of December 1991 and also that Strugar attacked -- ordered that attack on the 5th of December, 1991. The Supreme Command and the punishment for the 6th of December, 1991. Another subject that the Defence particularly wishes to deal with is the question of the attitude of the Supreme Command of the JNA and the protagonists of the events around Dubrovnik on the 6th of December, 1991. The Defence claimed that the investigation on the events of the 6th of December, 1991, or rather that the investigation on these events was taken over by the Supreme Command of the JNA, that the Supreme Command ordered Jokic to carry out an investigation, that Admiral Jokic upon orders of the Supreme Command carried out an investigation and informed the command about the results. All the reasons leading to such a conclusion were before the Trial Chamber. There was not a single other reason to conclude otherwise in the first instance proceedings. The order of the Supreme Command and the investigation carried out by Admiral Jokic excluded Strugar from the process of investigation and punishment. This rendered non-existent his material possibility to punish the perpetrators or his responsibility for -- failure to punish the perpetrators of the crime. The federal minister of defence ordered an urgent investigation and punishment of the perpetrators. Federal Minister Kadijevic ordered Jokic and Strugar to come to Belgrade on that day, the 6th of December, 1991, in order to report. Kadijevic ordered that Admiral Jokic carry out the investigation. That was a logical choice in view of the fact that all the units that took part in the said events were under his command. That is accepted by the Trial Chamber as well. Federal Minister Kadijevic informed five ambassadors of western countries on the same day, on the 6th of December, 1991, that he ordered an investigation and that whoever violated an order would be arrested and punished. All of this is contained in the case files. These facts are not denied by the Trial Chamber either. The Trial Chamber finds that on orders from Kadijevic, Jokic takes specific steps in the investigation that had been ordered. He asks for reports from higher-ranking officers of his command. He replaces the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic. Jokic takes statements from the commanders of companies that took part in the attack, precisely those company commanders that had the equipment that could imperil the old city, specifically Captain Nesic, the commander of anti-armour company from Zarkovica, and Jeremic, the commander of the 120-millimetre mortar battery. Admiral Jokic also calls Captain Kovacevic, who, together with Captains Nesic and Jeremic and 8th of December, 1991, come to the staff of the 9th Military Naval Sector. The report of Captain Nesic is contained in the case file. The commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic who was replaced by Jokic on the 6th of December, 1991, was also asked to make a statement at the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector about what had happened on that day, the 6th of December, 1991. Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic makes this statement already on the 6th of December, 1991, at 1400 hours at the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector where he had been asked to come. That is the statement where he mentions that Admiral Jokic indeed on the 5th of December was at the meeting in Kupari when the order on Srdj was planned and ordered. Acting on Kadijevic's orders, Admiral Jokic informs the General Staff of the JNA, namely, the operations department of the JNA, about what happened on the 6th of December, 1991, the measures that he took, and the measures that he intends to take. Admiral Jokic acting on Kadijevic's orders established a commission of high-ranking officers of the 9th Military Naval Sector that he sent to Dubrovnik in order to establish what the damage incurred was. On the 9th of December, 1991, Jokic sends a report to the Supreme Command. In this report, Jokic informs Admiral Brovet, the deputy federal minister of defence, about the following: That in the 9th Military Naval Sector a commission was established in order to determine the circumstances and damage inflicted upon the old city and that that commission toured the old city of Dubrovnik on the 8th of December, 1991. Furthermore, that the commission established that many buildings mentioned in this report were damaged. Furthermore, that the registered damage is not of larger proportions. Further on, that they cannot establish the origin of the damage. Also, that they cannot establish who the perpetrators of the damage inflicted upon the Old Town of Dubrovnik are. Along with this report, Admiral Jokic submits to Brovet, or rather, to Kadijevic a video cassette that the commission taped on the damage inflicted upon the old city on the 6th of December, 1991. There are many other circumstances that speak of the measures and activities taken by Admiral Jokic. The key fact is that Veljko Kadijevic, federal secretary for national defence, ordered Admiral Jokic to conduct an investigation on the events of the 6th of December, 1991. The Defence believes that this fact is of key importance for assessing the role of Strugar in the investigation and punishment. There is not a shred of evidence that Strugar was ordered to take part in the investigation. There is not a single reason to believe that Strugar believed that he should carry out the investigation. There is not a single reason for Strugar to believe that he should be involved in this investigation. In Strugar's presence, the man who embodies the Supreme Command of the JNA issues an order to Admiral Jokic to carry out an investigation and report on its results. The effect of the order of the Supreme Command to Admiral Jokic to conduct an investigation abolishes every possibility for Strugar to conduct some parallel investigation of his own apart from the investigation that is carried out upon orders from the highest instance in the JNA. The effect of the order of the Supreme Command to Admiral Jokic to conduct an investigation has the effect of a ban on anyone else carrying out the investigation. The principle of singleness of command in the JNA does not allow for the possibility that two identical tasks can be issued to two different units or commands to be carried out along parallel lines. That is confirmed by the behaviour of Admiral Jokic who submits all reports in relation to the undertaken investigation only to the Supreme Command. He did not submit these reports on the investigation carried out to Strugar. The Trial Chamber finds something that not a single trier of fact could find, that the order of Kadijevic does not mean anything for Strugar, and that he should carry out his own investigation regardless of the direct and explicit order of the highest commander of the JNA. As a matter of fact, the Trial Chamber even believes that Strugar was supposed to oppose Kadijevic's order or to conduct a parallel investigation. This kind of a position taken by the Trial Chamber is in fundamental disagreement with the basic postulates upon which military organisations rests. An order in an army, especially an order of the Supreme Military Command is not subject to discussion, debate, and non-acceptance. The only order that can be refused is an order to commit a crime which was not the substance of Kadijevic's order to Strugar. The key factor that led the Trial Chamber to believe that Strugar did not carry out the investigation is the alleged confession made to Colm Doyle that he had ordered the attack against Srdj which again closes the circle of illogical, impossible and unreasonable findings brought by the Trial Chamber. The Defence claims that not a -- that no reasonable trier of fact can conclude that Strugar had the material possibility to carry out an investigation and punish the perpetrators of the events of the 6th of December, 1991, primarily in view of the reasons pertaining to the role of the Supreme Command of the JNA in the matter. The Appeals Chamber asked in writing for clarification regarding the civilian status of Mato Valjalo and Ivo Vlasica, and that is to say the civilians who on the 6th of December, 1991, were injured in the old city. The Defence is going to state its views on that as well. The findings of the Trial Chamber are also erroneous in relation to the civilian status of Mato Valjalo on the 6th of December, 1991, when he was allegedly wounded in the old city because this is not adequate in terms of the evidence presented. As for Ivo Vlasica, the polemic on the type of injuries sustained by him was brought to an end when error number 43 in paragraph 61 was withdrawn in the appeal brief of the Defence. Sorry, my mistake, it is 53. The Defence only challenges the status of Mato Valjalo. Valjalo testified that on the 6th of December, 1991, in the morning, he was returning home after his tour of duty at the Crisis Staff. The evidence accepted by the Trial Chamber indicates that Mato Valjalo was assigned to work at the Crisis Staff and that during the attack against Dubrovnik he drove members of the Crisis Staff to different war assignments. That means that from the 15th of September, 1991, Mato Valjalo was mobilised and engaged from a military point of view. That also means that Mato Valjalo was allegedly wounded as he was returning from a duty that is directly related to the war effort of one of the warring parties. That fact denies his status of a civilian person. All of this is confirmed by the decision made by the secretariat for health, social welfare, labour, veterans and invalids affairs, the administration for veterans and invalid affairs, recognising to Mato Valjalo the status of a military -- war military invalid. That decision was issued in a procedure prescribed by law by the state organ in charge. The Defence recalls that in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, where laws are published as well as other legal decisions, it is called Narodne Novine, the number is 33/92 dated the 12th of June, 1992. In this official gazette, the Law on the Protection of Military and Civilian War Invalids was published. According to that law, there are the following categories of persons that are given protection: War military invalid, peacetime military invalid and civilian invalids of war. Civilian invalids of war, according to Article 8, paragraph 1, item 2 of the mentioned law are persons whose organism sustained injuries up to 20 per cent due to their injuries related to war incidents, bombing, the explosion of ordinance, a stray bullet, and the like. It is obvious that Mato Valjalo does not belong to that category, a civilian invalid of war, or rather, that he did not have the status of a civilian when he was wounded. If we try to remain consistent with the provisions of this law, the conclusion would be different because he was recognised as a military war invalid and the last thing that I wish to point out, in particular, is that the sentencing issue. The Defence also wishes to point out certain errors in sentencing that the Trial Chamber made in relation to General Strugar. When determining a sentence, the Trial Chamber failed to take into account certain facts or did not give sufficient weight to certain facts and circumstances that had to be taken into account when imposing a sentence. The Trial Chamber was wrong to dismiss Strugar's expression of remorse, and sincere regret. The alleged role of the accused in the attack on Srdj cannot be used in this argument to dismiss his remorse. The Trial Chamber repeatedly established that the Old Town was not the target of the attack allegedly ordered by Strugar. The Defence further believes that the Trial Chamber failed to give sufficient and appropriate weight to General Strugar's sincere remorse over the suffering of the people in Dubrovnik which General Strugar expressed to the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber took into account as mitigating circumstances his personal and family situation, his good character, and his voluntary surrender. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber gave insufficient weight to these mitigating factors. The eight-year sentence imposed on Strugar had to be mitigated by an appropriate assessment of the meaning of the mitigating circumstances. The Trial Chamber also erred when it failed to take into account as a special mitigating circumstance the serious health conditions of Pavle Strugar, something that must be taken into account as a special and exceptional mitigating circumstance. In addition to vascular dementia, memory loss and depression, as stated in the judgement, at the same time, Strugar suffers from a chronic insufficiency of the kidney, bilateral nephrotic disruptions to the functioning of the kidney, spondylosis of the neck and arthrosis, spondyloarthrosis of the lower spinal column, osteoarthrosis of the hips, prostatic adenoma and ulcer. Evidence had already been led on all these at the time the sentence was reached. The medical experts of both the Defence and the Prosecution established a prognosis as to Mr. Strugar's general state of health. There has been a constant and ongoing deterioration. The fact is in evidence that in December 2005, Mr. Strugar underwent surgery in Podgorica during which he was given an artificial right hip. Based on a neuropsychological report of the Neurology Institute of Serbia's KC from April 2006, it is obvious that Strugar suffered further deterioration of his already impaired visual perceptive and construction abilities in terms of 3D perception, that his attention span was further shortened and impaired as well as his phonemic fluency. Now, in relation to all phonemes. There is a delay in his powers of verbal recall and his executive functioning also shows a deterioration in relation to the time at which previous tests were conducted. Likewise, there is a specialist report by a urologist from the same period in 2006 confirming all his chronic conditions and problems with the kidneys and prostate. All of the findings from that period were tendered into evidence in a Defence filing, a confidential Defence filing dated the 11th of September, 2006. Further, there was a detailed institute drawn up by the Institute for Orthopaedics and Traumatology of Serbia's KC dated the 8th of May, 2007. Pavle Strugar received a recommendation for surgical treatment of both knees and the left hip in the sense of being given a full implant. Serious degenerative changes down the entire length of the neck section of his spine were established. At level C-5 and C-6, there is hardly any joint room left. At levels C-6 and C-7, there is no joint room left at all and this area is also affected by severe ankylosis. Likewise, there is an LS image of his spine showing degenerations to all of his vertebra. At the L-5 level, there is discarthrosis. This is another report that was tendered by the Defence in a filing dated the 10th of May, 2007. Another thing that warrants pointing out is the report which is a summary of the health situation of Mr. Strugar drawn up by Dr. Falke from the UN detention unit on the 21st of January, 2008. This report confirms all the conditions found in Mr. Strugar. Based on all of this, the Defence submits that Mr. Strugar's health is something that must be taken into account as a special mitigating circumstance and given appropriate weight. The Defence believes that Mr. Strugar's health is an exceptional situation, constitutes an exception, especially in view of the position put forward by the Appeals Chamber. The Trial Chamber erred as it failed to take into account as a mitigating circumstance, Pavle Strugar's age. In two and a half months, Strugar will be turning 75. As stated in the Plavcic sentence, it is indisputable that a weakening of the body that can be a result of aging often leads to additional difficulty in serving a sentence. It is more difficult for an elderly person to serve a sentence than for a younger person. It is just as indisputable that once an aged person is released, they do not have much of a chance of a decent life afterwards. In Strugar's case, a weakening of the body is particularly prominent because of his many illnesses that have been diagnosed. Bearing in mind his age and his poor health, and in view of the sentence that was imposed, objectively speaking, Strugar has no hope of a quality life once he is released, if, indeed, he is ever released while still alive. One thing is the his age and the other is the progress --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do you need, because we will have to break in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm about to conclude in two or three minutes, if I may be allowed to continue for that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is Strugar's age on the one hand and the progress of his illness on the other, and both have been predicted by medical experts. Any prolonged stay in prison would be filled with pain, humiliation and suffering. He also has a wife that he is emotionally attached to and has been married to for over 50 years. She is also suffering from a number of serious health conditions and has been unable to visit him for a number of years now. It is because of all this that the Defence believes that Strugar's case has all the hallmarks of an exceptional case where factors such as age and poor health must be taken into account as a significant mitigating circumstance. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber failed to impose an appropriate sentence on Strugar by disregarding a number of mitigating circumstances altogether while awarding insufficient weight to others. The Defence believes that were the facts of the case properly assessed and all the mitigating circumstances taken into account, the sentence imposed would be significantly milder or more lenient. The Defence believes that the Appeals Chamber should revise and significantly reduce the sentence imposed on Strugar in the light of this appeal. We also move that the Appeals Chamber consider all errors of law and fact committed by the Trial Chamber and pointed out in the Defence's brief. The Defence moves that Strugar be acquitted on all charges on which he was found guilty on the 31st of January, 2005. More specifically, under 7(1) [as interpreted] and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, the Defence moves that Strugar be retried or alternatively that his sentence be significantly reduced. Thank you. I'm sorry, I said 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, not 7(1). Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Rodic. We are now going to break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 11.35. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. You have a question, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. I have a question to the counsel for the Defence. I listened in interest to your argument according to which the General Staff ordered Admiral Jokic to carry out an investigation of the totality of the events that took place at the relevant dates. You argued that once such an order was given to Admiral Jokic, that then under the general principles governing relations within the military, and proper arrangements of order and discipline, General Strugar would have been exonerated from carrying an investigation of his own. Could you elaborate on this a little bit more and also perhaps tell me, tell the Court, why couldn't -- why -- should General Strugar and could he have carried out a sequential investigation of his own, namely after the investigation by Admiral Jokic would have been concluded. Could you give us clarification on this point? Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honour. What I can say is response is this. As I have already mentioned, the governing principle of every army that I can say specifically about the JNA because that was at issue here, the Law on Defence and the entire legislation governing the operation of the army and the rules of service as well have as the underlying principle single command and subordination. When the highest level, in this case, it was General Kadijevic as the Supreme Commander and Minister of Defence, issues a direct order to an officer as to what he should do, as he issued an order, in this case, to General Jokic to conduct an investigation, he thereby designated General Jokic for the reason that his units were involved in the event, for the reason that the area is within the territorial coverage of Jokic's units. He designated him as the most reliable and the most competent to conduct this investigation. The commander of the 2nd Operation Group is dozens of kilometres away in Trebinje, that is the command that commands over several corps. General Jokic, following the same principle of command and singleness of command acted in the way he did, in the way he was ordered. He conducted an investigation, he wrote three reports that he sent directly to General Kadijevic from which he had received his orders whereas he did not even inform General Strugar of this either by sending him a copy of the reports or addressing to him a combat report saying, I have taken such and such action and reported it to the Supreme Commander, General Kadijevic. Therefore, General Strugar was completely out of the picture in this investigation. He was completely side-lined by the order of General Kadijevic and had no access whatsoever to any of the findings of the investigation. It was only General Kadijevic, as the minister, and as the Supreme Commander who was able to change anything in this line of action or to order a new investigation if he was not satisfied or if he wanted additional information. Therefore, General Strugar could not get involved without express orders and permission because he was present when General Kadijevic gave these orders to General Jokic. Any later investigation, any subsequent investigation would also require orders from the higher level, in this case, General Kadijevic, who issued orders for the first investigation. Those are certainly the military realities and the military rules in the Yugoslav People's Army that govern this matter and regulate it in this way. We provided more detailed reasoning and arguments in our appellate brief invoking evidence in this case and jurisprudence in this Tribunal related to the military realities and military practice rules and laws. Let me also draw your attention to something I've mentioned before. Minister Kadijevic who was in contact with the highest officials of western countries through their ambassadors informed them, based on the findings he received from Jokic. He informed them of the orders to conduct an investigation and that is also mentioned in our brief. Thank you, Your Honour. Would this suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rodic, I listened to your submissions with great interest, your submissions related to sentencing and to mitigating circumstances. Based on your submissions, could we come to the conclusion that the minimum capacity of Strugar was taken into account when determining the sentence and when establishing mitigating circumstances? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is true that in the Trial Chamber's judgement, it is stated that one of the mitigating circumstances was the poor health of General Strugar, specifically vascular dementia, memory loss, and depression. That is what is stated in the trial judgement. However, it is the position of the Defence that although at the moment of sentencing the Trial Chamber was aware that Strugar also suffers from various other health conditions, which in their totality, together with the two specifically named by the Trial Chamber, amount to extremely poor and deteriorating health. The Defence believes that the Trial Chamber did not lend sufficient weight to all the medical evidence before them and that is why they did not attach sufficient weight to the mitigating circumstances arising from the health condition of General Strugar. We now provided you with additional information from reports dating back to 2005 when an artificial hip was implanted to him. We provided further evidence of the deterioration of his health since 2005 established by later medical examination. And this deterioration in his condition is consistent with the testimony of medical experts of the Defence and the medical experts of the Prosecution saying that as a result of all his health conditions combined, a further deterioration would ensue compared to the already poor status of his health. That is all contained in our brief and in our reports, in our filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have two questions. Firstly, since you have not expanded on the fitness of Strugar to stand trial, can you tell us if you've decided not to raise that point again or is it just that you decided not to deal with that today at this hearing? And can you also tell us whether General Strugar could not have requested Admiral Jokic's report following the orders of Kadijevic? Couldn't he have requested to see these reports in order to take action possibly?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to your first question concerning the fitness of General Strugar to stand trial. We have dealt with that in detail in the appellate brief, in our grounds of appeal on the trial judgement, and we have nothing to add today to the arguments presented there. For the sake of expediency and following the guidelines of the Appeals Chamber, we chose to put the emphasis today on other key issues from which all the further errors we quoted in our appellate's brief are derived. In response to your second question, if I understood it properly, you ask me if General Strugar had been able to request Admiral Jokic's report following the orders of General Kadijevic. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask whether he did it. I asked whether he would have been in a position to do it considering the rules prevailing in the military. Could he have done it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the rules prevailing in the JNA and all the regulations, even if we set aside this particular situation of General Strugar and General Jokic, I will describe to you what the situation is in the Yugoslav People's Army. A superior commander orders a lower commander, a battalion commander or let's say a company commander who is two levels below him to perform a certain task, to submit a report, prepare a report. The battalion commander who is superior to the company commander but is lower in rank than the brigade commander or the corps commander who issued the task in the first place has no right to get involved. He has no right to require the person who received the orders to conduct an investigation or prepare a report. He is not entitled to get involved in the implementation of that order. According to military regulations, he has no right to do that because that would violate the principle of single command. This has special weight attached to it because in this particular situation, we are dealing with the Supreme Commander who is a superior to all military personnel, all the generals under his command. So when he issues an order to anyone at a lower level, regardless of how lower, and tells them that they are to communicate directly with him, without saying expressly that he is also to inform other units or other persons, then no one else has the right to get involved in that communication or in the execution of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Judge Meron has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm not entirely pleased with the answer you gave to the question posed by our Presiding Judge. Her question was not whether General Strugar could get involved in the matter, the question was once the investigation, if I understand it correctly, once the investigation was over, the reports had been written, obviously General Strugar knew about the investigations. You told us that the order to investigate was in fact given Admiral Jokic in the presence of General Strugar. Once he was in a way interested and involved, couldn't he have asked the General Staff to provide him with copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in a situation when an order is issued to Admiral Jokic to carry out an investigation, I'm going to describe the situation now. General Kadijevic calls General Strugar to come with Admiral Jokic to see him in Belgrade and to report to him. The overriding military principle is that the immediate superior of the person who is being called in to report, in this case, it is Admiral Jokic, at that point, Strugar, as commander of the 2nd Operations Group is his immediate superior, so the principle is that Jokic goes along with his immediate superior to report to the ultimate superior. So when Kadijevic called in Jokic, he observed military regulations governing reporting. So Strugar is present with his subordinate officer when General Kadijevic issues an order directly to his subordinate Admiral Jokic and makes him the person in charge to communicate in terms of this order. General Kadijevic as the Supreme Commander certainly could have, had he deemed it necessary in that situation, issued an additional order, namely, you will inform your immediate superior Strugar about what it is you will report to me, in part or in some other way. However, Kadijevic as the Supreme Commander did not do that. He took over everything, as well as this direct communication with Admiral Jokic. So General Strugar, in response to your first question when I was providing an answer, General Strugar really has no possibility, in terms of the principle of singleness in command of the JNA, to interfere and to ask Admiral Jokic, let me see a copy of the report, submit a copy to me too, or to ask Kadijevic to see what it was that Jokic had said. In both such cases, in terms of singleness of command in the JNA, this would have been held against him, why he was not observing the order that had been issued that did not involve him and that he could not interfere with. Certainly, Kadijevic, as the Supreme Commander had he deemed it necessary, in any form by way of assistance or whatever, he could have, through this order on carrying out an investigation, involved both of them and he could have entrusted it to both of them. Or, he could have even sent in an independent team of officers independent of the two of them from the secretariat and he could have ordered them to carry out the investigation. So my answer is that Strugar, in this situation, in this kind of a situation, he cannot ask Kadijevic or Jokic about the results of the investigation carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Rodic. I don't think there are any further questions from the Bench, I now give the floor to the Prosecution for their response. You have an hour to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Trial Chamber's findings were reasonable and the Defence has failed to show that the Trial Chamber committed any reversible error. I will address two main issues in ground 1 of the Defence appeal. First, I will show that the Trial Chamber's finding that the accused ordered the attack on Srdj was supported by the evidence. Second, I will respond to your question concerning the status of the victims. My colleague, Mr. Tracol, will address grounds 2 and 3 of the Defence appeal, and Ms. Brady will speak to sentence, ground 4. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was correct to find that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj. Before I respond to the details of the Defence submissions this morning which concentrate on specific pieces of evidence, I would like to touch on the extensive evidence and factual findings that underlie the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Strugar gave the order for the attack. These facts fall under three headings: Before, during, and after the attack. What was happening before the attack is important because it sets the stage for Strugar's order. The military realities, the diplomatic situation and the planning show that the order to attack Srdj originated at the highest levels of the JNA with the commander of the 2 OG, General Strugar. The military realities are important because the JNA operates under a single unified command. This is not based on conjecture. The Trial Chamber's findings in this regard are based on extensive evidence and I would direct you to paragraphs 393 to 405 of the trial judgement. Singular unified command is essentially a top-down structure where orders are formulated at the top and transmitted down the chain of command to subordinates. This structure supports the conclusion that the order for the attack originated with Strugar as the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. The diplomatic context is also significant because it too points to high-level authorisation for this attack. On 23 November 1991, the highest Serbian and Croatian authorities concluded the Geneva Accord which called for an unconditional cease-fire and for the withdrawal of JNA forces from Dubrovnik. On 5 December, Admiral Jokic, Strugar's subordinate, met with Croatian ministers to iron out the details of this cease-fire which was scheduled to commence on 6 December 1991 at 12.00 noon. Against this backdrop, at the brink of the cease-fire, senior officers of the 9 VPS including Jokic's Chief of Staff Zec and Captain Kovacevic, who was commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, met in the late afternoon of 5 December in Kupari. They devised a coordinated battle plan to seize Mount Srdj before the cease-fire was to come into effect. That same evening, Kovacevic visited Strugar's headquarters. Much later, Kovacevic met with his subordinate commanders to inform them about the attack, to pass the information down the chain. He told them that the attack had been approved by "the superior command." The Trial Chamber concluded that the order could not have originated with anyone other than the commander of the 2 OG given the command structure of the JNA, and particularly in light of the negotiations, in light of that impending cease-fire. I would refer you in this regard, for example, to paragraphs 89 and 167 of the judgement. Turning now to the events that took place during the attack itself. These facts prove that Strugar ordered the attack. In the early morning of 6 December 1991, ground troops of Kovacevic's battalion commenced their assault against Srdj. They attracted Croatian defensive fire from the wider town of Dubrovnik. Instead of responding against Croatian military positions where these military positions were threatening their assault on Srdj, the JNA artillery fired at the Old Town of Dubrovnik. There were no military targets in the Old Town. The Trial Chamber finds that particularly -- sorry, the Trial Chamber finds at paragraph 345 that they did so deliberately, indiscriminately and extensively over a prolonged period of time. The Old Town was attacked for ten and a half hours on the 6th of December, 1991, killing and injuring civilians and damaging historically and culturally important buildings. It's not surprising that the attack on Dubrovnik immediately attracted international attention. At 7.00 a.m., Strugar received a telephone call from his superior, the federal secretary of national defence, General Kadijevic who had already received a protest from the ECMM. Kadijevic was angry about the course of the events and demanded that Strugar and Jokic travel to Belgrade that day to report on the attack. In the Trial Chamber's view, and you can find this at paragraph 427, the continuation of this attack during the 6th of December was "telling and compelling" evidence of the true state of Strugar's orders. The Trial Chamber found in particular that Strugar did not issue any orders to stop the attack. If Strugar wasn't responsible for the initial order, then the Trial Chamber would have expected him to stop an unauthorised attack, particularly -- particularly after it started to get in the Trial Chamber's words "gravely out of hand." If he wasn't responsible for the initial order, he would have put a stop to it. Instead, the Trial Chamber found that between 12.00 and 12.30 p.m., Strugar met with Colm Doyle, an ECMM monitor. He admitted to Doyle at that moment that he fired on the city of Dubrovnik. This was before he travelled to Belgrade. This was before the sham investigation. At that stage in the heat of the moment, during the attack, Strugar told the ECMM monitor that he fired on the city of Dubrovnik. The results that came after the attack provide further confirmation of the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj. If Strugar had not given the order, then again we would expect to see him taking vigorous action against his undisciplined subordinates for initiating an unauthorised attack that would -- that got him into trouble with his superiors in Belgrade. Instead, the facts as found by the Trial Chamber show that Strugar approved of the military action. For example, Strugar invited Kovacevic to nominate outstanding soldiers for awards in relation to their participation in the attack of the 6 December 1991. He did not intervene to stop the promotion of Kadijevic. In sum, the Trial Chamber correctly looked at the totality of the evidence in reaching its conclusion that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj. I would like to turn now to address two of the Defence's main challenges raised this morning concerning the order to attack. First, with regard to Strugar's admission, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 164 that Strugar admitted to ECMM monitor Doyle that he ordered the attack on Srdj. The Trial Chamber accepted Doyle's evidence that when he met with Strugar around noon on 6 December, Strugar explained to him that he responded to Croatian provocations in Bosnia-Herzegovina by "firing on the city of Dubrovnik." It's true, as the Defence points out, that Strugar does not use the word Srdj. The plain meaning of his words is that Strugar ordered an attack on the city of Dubrovnik. However, the Trial Chamber was entitled to look at Strugar's statement in the context of the other evidence and to take an interpretation that was more favourable to the accused. I say it's more favourable because Srdj was a legitimate military target. This is a more favourable interpretation than an attack on the city of Dubrovnik itself. This was a correct approach. In any event, the Trial Chamber acknowledged at paragraph 343 that an attack on Srdj would necessarily draw Croatian fire from their defensive positions and that an artillery exchange involving the city of Dubrovnik was an integral part of the Srdj attack. This was a reasonable interpretation and the Defence has not shown that the Trial Chamber erred. The Trial Chamber took into account the questions of interpretation raised by the Defence this morning. It took into account all of these challenges and it made an -- it took an interpretation favourable to the Defence in that regard. In accepting Doyle's evidence concerning the meeting, the Trial Chamber rejected the evidence of Defence witness Svicevic. The Trial Chamber simply did not believe him. It gave reasons. The Trial Chamber found that his attempt to re-interpret his notes by moving around their order was patently false. The Defence again has not shown this to be unreasonable. Turning to the second point. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that Strugar ordered the attack did not depend on whether Jokic, his subordinate, attended the planning meeting. At the meeting in Kupari on the evening of 5 December, senior officers of the 9 VPS planned the attack on Srdj. Defence witness Jovanovic attended this meeting and testified that Jokic was present. Jokic was recalled to testify in rebuttal and emphatically denied that allegation. The Trial Chamber expressed reservations about Jovanovic's evidence because he had a personal interest in putting Jokic in that meeting, and because his evidence about the meeting did not accord with the military realities of the situation. In the end, the Trial Chamber considered at paragraph 88 that Jokic's attendance at the meeting was not determinative of its decision and left the issue "in balance." The Trial Chamber's approach was reasonable. The Defence wants Jokic at the meeting for the purpose of arguing that Jokic was involved in the planning of the attack and the implementation of the attack, in order to show that Strugar was not involved. However, their conclusion does not flow from that premise. Putting Jokic at the meeting does not show that Strugar was not involved. It does not show that Strugar didn't give the order. The Trial Chamber addresses the implications of Jokic's involvement at paragraph 98 of the judgement where the Trial Chamber reflects on Jovanovic's evidence and rejects the argument that the plan was "hatched and implemented by the 9 VPS including Admiral Jokic, without the accused's knowledge and contrary to his orders." The Trial Chamber acknowledged in paragraph 88 that its approach had effects on Jokic's credibility. Although the Prosecution argued on the basis of Jokic's evidence that he was not present at the meeting, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the issue could remain in balance shows that it did not accept Jokic on this issue. Throughout the judgement, the Trial Chamber treats Jokic's evidence with caution. The Trial Chamber was clearly aware of the effects of Jokic's parallel proceedings. It looks at the cross-examination of Jokic on the basis of his prior interviews. The Trial Chamber accepts Jokic's evidence on some issues and rejects it on others. In some instances, the Trial Chamber looks for independent corroboration of Jokic's account of the events. The Trial Chamber's determination that Jokic's attendance at that meeting could remain in balance was reasonable in the circumstances and it reflected the Trial Chamber's already cautious view of Jokic's evidence. The Defence has failed to show that the Trial Chamber's conclusions about the Kupari meeting were unreasonable. Ultimately, the evidence proved that Jokic [sic] gave the order to attack Srdj whether or not Jokic was present at that meeting. Sorry, I'd like to correct the transcript. The evidence proved that Strugar gave the order to attack Srdj. Thank you. Your Honours, in this case, the absence of a written order which might have answered some of the detailed questions posed by the Defence this morning is not surprising. Particularly given the sensitive diplomatic backdrop preceded attack, the international attention to the attack and the sham JNA investigation which followed. On the Trial Chamber's own findings in the judgement at paragraph 6 and 7, some relevant documents related to this case were not locatable. Some of the documentary evidence presented in this case was deliberately false and contrived. In these circumstances, the absence of a written order should not disturb. On the basis of the mutually-reinforcing evidence presented at trial, the Trial Chamber found that General Strugar ordered forces under his command to attack Srdj on 6 December 1991. Strugar admitted this to Doyle. The diplomatic circumstances, the military realities, the sequence of the events, the duration of the attack, and Strugar's approval of the participants' actions proves, in a logical and reasonable way that the attack was undertaken pursuant to Strugar's orders. Your Honours, the Defence has concentrated on this order as if, in the absence of this order, Strugar would be acquitted. That is not the case. Strugar's conviction would remain even if he hadn't given the order on the 5th of December. If it wasn't Strugar who gave the order to attack, then at 7.00 in the morning when Strugar learned from the telephone call from Kadijevic that forces under his command were undertaking an unauthorised assault in the area of Dubrovnik, undertaking unauthorised military combat action, then Strugar would have even more reason to be alarmed. He would be on more notice of the possibility of crimes, the real and reasonable risk that crimes were going to occur. I'd like to turn now to Your Honours' second question concerning the status of the victims. Mato Valjalo and Ivo Vlasica were both civilians. The Defence has not challenged the status of Vlasica on appeal. With regard to Mato Valjalo, the Prosecution has responded in detail to the Defence arguments concerning his status in our response brief. These arguments were also raised at trial.
