In the final trial brief at paragraphs 166 to 172, the Prosecution explained that Mato was not a member of the armed forces; he was a civilian working as a driver for the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff and he received his pension on that basis. This evidence was considered by the Trial Chamber which found that he was a civilian who was not taking an active part in the hostilities. This same person was also a named victim in the Jokic case and a similar conclusion was reached by the Jokic Trial Chamber and was affirmed on appeal. The second part of your question which asks whether a combatant can be a legitimate military target under international humanitarian law is slightly more complicated by the fact that although the Prosecution charged an international armed conflict and argued in our final trial brief that Croatia had achieved statehood by 6 December 1991, the Trial Chamber did not make a determinative finding on this issue. If the armed conflict were considered to be international, then a combatant would clearly be a lawful military target. In a non-international armed conflict, the label of "combatant" which carries with it rights to participate in the armed conflict and prisoner of war status does not specifically apply. However, it's of course still necessary to distinguish between members of the armed forces and other organised armed groups on one hand. Those are the people who are actually conducting hostilities on behalf of a party. It's important to distinguish them from civilians who are not. According to Additional Protocol II, Article 13, civilians who take a direct part in hostilities lose their protection against attack for the duration of their participation. This is equivalent to the definition in Common Article 3. Direct or active participation in hostilities requires a direct causal relationship between the activity and military harm to the enemy. In the language of the ICRC commentary, to take a direct part in hostilities means to engage in acts of war which, by their nature or purpose, are likely to cause actual harm to the personnel or materiel of the enemy armed forces. Civilians are often used as part of a war effort, but this does not turn a civilian into a legitimate military target. In this case, the Crisis Staff was not part of the armed forces. Even if it were, Mato Valjalo was not a member of the Crisis Staff and in his auxiliary position as a driver, he does not meet the test of taking a direct part in the hostilities. The domestic law characterisation of his pension does not determine and cannot determine his status for the purposes of international humanitarian law. Assuming just for the purposes of answering your question fully that one of these victims was a member of an organised armed group or the armed forces conducting the hostilities, then the answer would be yes, he would be a legitimate military target. If he was a civilian who was directly participating in the hostilities, then again, he could be legitimately targeted during the time of his participation. As a legitimate target, he would not be counted as a victim of an unlawful attack against civilians under Count 3 of the indictment. The Trial Chamber correctly found that both of these victims were civilians who were not taking an active part in the hostilities. These findings were reasonable and should be affirmed. Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my submissions, subject to any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no questions. Thank you, Ms. Baig. I think it is Mr. Tracol who is on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now respond to the second and third grounds of appeal of the Defence and I shall start off with a response to the third ground of appeal of the Defence. Given that the Defence presented no arguments this morning relating to the first element included in that of -- in the responsibility of a superior, i.e., the superior-subordinate relationship, I will not add anything to what has already been mentioned in our response brief. I shall also be very brief as regards the second element, i.e., responsibility of a superior and the mens rea standard. I would just like to point out that Strugar had reason to know that his subordinates were committing crimes and was informed of the attack based on the telephone call he got from General Kadijevic on the 6th of December at 7.00 in the morning. This is a conclusion of the Trial Chamber in its judgement in paragraph 418. This finding is safe in light of the wider context and the circumstances of the case. Strugar's forces had already shelled the Old Town in October and November 1991. The second key element is of course Jokic's testimony relating to Strugar's telephone call on the 6th of December at 7.00 in the morning. I shall just point out these two points, since the Defence presented no arguments this morning relating to the mens rea standard in the responsibility of a superior. Now, third element, the responsibility of a superior. Strugar did not take the necessary measures and reasonable action to prevent the crimes and punish the perpetrators. First of all, Strugar is criminally responsible for not having prevented the crimes. Here again, I point out that the Defence remained silent on this point, i.e., the responsibility of a superior and said nothing about this this morning. I shall therefore just point out the following: The conclusions of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 420 to 430 of the judgement whereby Strugar failed to take any effective measure from 7.00 in the morning are reasonable. And the Defence has demonstrated no error committed by the Trial Chamber in its analysis. I shall therefore simply point out three issues. The first is that Strugar's actions were all ineffective. Second point, Strugar gave no order to stop the attack on Srdj. Third point, the cease-fire was also ineffective. I shall say no more about the fact that Strugar did not prevent the crimes from being committed since the Defence presented no arguments on this topic this morning. But Strugar did not punish the perpetrators of the crimes either. The Trial Chamber rightly found in paragraph 446 of the judgement that Strugar did not punish the perpetrators, he conducted no investigation on the behaviour of his subordinates responsible for the shelling of the Old Town, and took no disciplinary measures against them in respect of the events of the 6th of December, 1991. Madam President, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber has provided detailed reasons for this in paragraph 436 of the judgement and stated that Jokic conducted a sham investigation which was not designed to reach the truth or to punish the perpetrators and this was done with the tacit approval of Strugar. Strugar does not even allege, let alone show, that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusions contained in the judgement. The Trial Chamber also correctly found in paragraph 439 of the judgement that Strugar was, and I quote: "... at the very least with his tacit approval, a participant in the arrangement by which Admiral Jokic undertook his sham investigation and sham disciplinary action and reported to the 1st Secretariat in a way which deflected responsibility for the damage to the Old Town from the JNA." The damage caused by the JNA. Strugar was not or did not think he was in a position to act or had not received an order not to intervene in the events that took place on the 6th of December. The fact that General Kadijevic delegated the duty to draft a report to Jokic does not mean that Strugar should have shied away from his own duty to punish. Every responsible commander must make sure that the crimes are correctly investigated. Madam President, Your Honours, contrary to what Mr. Rodic has stated, Strugar was not set aside or side-lined. The Defence is merely repeating the arguments relating to Strugar's exclusion by General Kadijevic, arguments that were already presented at trial. The first instance judges have looked into these arguments presented by the Defence in paragraph 438 of the judgement and the first trial judges have rejected these arguments in paragraph 439 and 442 of the judgement. Madam president, Your Honours, it is inconceivable to imagine that a superior would not have to perform his obligation by the mere order from someone else. If the commission of a crime is covered by someone else, the Defence argument means that a superior would be under no -- under no obligation to intervene. In this particular case, Strugar was under the obligation to be kept informed, to -- in line with the military doctrine of the JNA and he needed to be informed by the two levels in the army below him. Zorc, who was the Prosecution's expert, presented a report on the matter; P204 is the exhibit number. He also testified on this point during the trial and I would like to refer the Trial Chamber to the transcript number 6595, 6596, 6592, 6593.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 6692, 6693.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Judge Meron pointed out, Strugar was interested in this investigation and its results. Madam President, Your Honours, the findings of the Trial Chamber are well-founded in light of the events that occurred after that. Rather than punish Kovacevic, Strugar did not oppose Kovacevic's promotion even though he had the authority to do it as the Judges of the Trial Bench clearly indicated in paragraph 481 of the judgement -- 441. The commander of the 472nd Motorised Brigade promoted him to Captain First Class with a retroactive effect as of the 11th of the November, after the shelling of the Old Town in November 1991. Kovacevic was promoted on the 14th of December, i.e., only eight days after the 6th of December, the date on which the Old Town was shelled. It is clear that Strugar decided not to use those instruments he had at his disposal to oppose Kovacevic's promotion. Strugar has shied away from his obligation to punish the perpetrators. Kovacevic's promotion is not the sole proof of Strugar's dereliction of duty to punish the perpetrators. This promotion shows two things: A, that Kovacevic's promotion provides a circumstantial piece of evidence which shows in an indirect manner that Strugar did not give the order to stop the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December at 7.00 in the morning. Madam President, Your Honours, if Kovacevic had -- did not comply with the order, Strugar would then have taken disciplinary measures against him rather than failing to stop his promotion. Second, Kovacevic's promotion is so astonishing that it further proves that Strugar endorsed and approved the attack on Srdj. Lastly, the Trial Chamber made a specific finding in paragraph 441 of the judgement that the visit of General Panic, who was deputy chief of General Staff in the JNA to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade took place. The Trial Chamber did not need to resolve the question of the date of his visit since the importance of the visit lies in that at the time of the visit, Strugar invited Kovacevic, and I quote paragraph 441 of the judgement: "To nominate outstanding participants in the events of the 6th of the December." The Trial Chamber reasonably accepted Jokic's testimony on this point. Madam President, Your Honours, I have completed my arguments in response to the third ground of appeal of the Defence. I can now briefly look into the second ground of appeal of the Defence but I suggest to merely respond to the first question which was put to the parties, if the Bench agrees with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can proceed and Mr. Shahabuddeen would like to put a question to you in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber rightly found in paragraph 483 of the - 283 of the judgement that the issue as to whether a standard lower than that of direct intent may also suffice does not arise in this case. To answer your question, the position of the Prosecution is as follows: The standard relating to mens rea in the attack against civilian objects should be identical to the standard used in attacks against civilians on which the Appeals Chamber has already ruled in paragraph 140 of the Galic judgement relating -- this is the same as wilful damage, to cultural property. According to the Prosecution, a mens rea standard of indirect intent suffices for attack on civilian objects. The accused must be aware of the substantial likelihood that unlawful damage would result to civilian objects. I have completed my response to the first question put to me by the Bench. I can answer any question if the Bench so wishes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, I have been interested in the point made by colleagues and by Defence counsel about investigations having been ordered at a higher level of the JNA and about that operating on the basis of the principle of unity of command to neutralise, as it were, any obligation of the commander to prevent or to punish his subordinates. Do I correctly understand your answer to this proposition to be this, that yes, the obligation of a commander to prevent or punish can be overborne by action taken at a higher level on the chain of command on the principle of unity of command but not where, according to you, the action taken at the higher level was always, and to the knowledge of the commander, intended to be by way of a sham. It was not real, and that is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution is that the commander of an army has always, subject to the idea that there is command responsibility, always has the obligation to punish if he is informed or is aware of the crimes that have been committed. The fact that an investigation is ordered by a superior to a subordinate of the commander in question does not relieve the superior of the obligation. That is the principle at hand. Of course it is important to apply this to the facts of the case. The other important element in this case, according to us, is the principle of unity of command and the obligation of the superiors to be kept informed, and to that, they need to be kept informed two levels down which means that the subordinates also have the obligation to inform their superiors two levels up. These two elements confirm that Strugar was under the obligation to punish his subordinates. Of course if we look into the facts of the case, the mens rea element in the responsibility of a superior was established since Strugar, as of the 6th of December at 7.00 in the morning was informed of the commission of these crimes, and it is this knowledge which should have triggered, on his part, an investigation into the crimes that had been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron has a question to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence argued that General Strugar was taken out of the loop, as to say, by the higher orders issued directly to Admiral Jokic to investigate. He also argued that at no time did General Strugar receive copies of those reports which were produced. I understood him to say that under the military principles of military discipline, he was not in a position to ask for copies and/or to intervene in any way. Now, how could he then have taken, General Strugar, have taken steps to further investigate and/or punish if he was not aware of the contents of the reports of Admiral Jokic? If the function of investigation and punishment was otherwise handled and this was by orders of the supreme military authority, what exactly should he have done? And I'm aware of the content of paragraph 445 of the trial judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the arguments of the Defence have already been presented at trial. These arguments are nothing new. The Trial Chamber has scrutinised these and has dismissed them. I would like to draw your attention not to paragraph 44 -- 445 of the judgement, but to the conclusions of the judgement in paragraph 443. In the normal chain of command of the JNA, a communication on the part of Jokic -- Kadijevic to Jokic had to go through the commander of the 2nd Operational Group and the commander of this group was, in this case, Strugar. To complete my answer, it is just inconceivable, given the military doctrine of the JNA and the rules whereby the superior needed to be kept inform two levels up and two levels down that Strugar was not informed of the contents of the reports provided by Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, how do you read, then, paragraph 445 of the judgement? And where Strugar understood the orders issued to the Admiral as intended to put him aside, the General says he should never -- have tried to undertake the investigative orders. Can you tell me a little bit more about it so I could be comfortable with this idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even if General Kadijavic asked Admiral Jokic to go out on a mission and cover these events, this mission in substance does not enable General Strugar from avoiding his obligation which was to punish his subordinates. All the elements of a superior are met in this case. General Strugar was under the obligation to punish his subordinates for the crimes that had been committed, and the fact that an investigation had been conducted by higher levels and General Kadijevic and one of -- and Jokic, one of his subordinates, does not mean that Strugar was not under the obligation to punish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Has anyone been punished -- was anyone punished under the original reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. None of Jokic's subordinates has been punished after the sham investigation, I should say, which was conducted by Admiral Jokic. This, I think, is sufficiently evocative and demonstrates that the obligation to punish was not complied with. Only Jovanovic was punished and he was temporarily punished and this can in no way be qualified as satisfactory in regard of Strugar's obligation to punish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tracol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: As far as the rest of the presentation is concerned, yes, I shall now give the floor to my colleague, Helen Brady, who will address the fourth ground of appeal of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Brady, how much time do you need for your presentation?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can be extremely brief in response to the Defence's fourth ground of the appeal on sentence. I should be no more than two or three minutes at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: In our submission, the sentence imposed of eight years is not excessive as the Defence argues and in fact, as we will argue in our own Prosecution appeal against sentence this afternoon, it was precisely the opposite. It was manifestly inadequate. The reason why I can be so brief this morning in responding to his submissions on sentence is that most of the issues that he raises in fact overlap with issues that we raise in our sentence appeal and this is especially regarding comparisons to the Jokic case and his arguments about Strugar's alleged apology at the time of the events and also during the trial. So because of the overlap, I don't intend to now directly respond to these arguments but rather I'll address them this afternoon when I present our arguments on why his sentence was, in our submission, too low. However, he has also raised a few discrete points which do not arise in our appeal, and especially he argues that the Trial Chamber did not give weight or sufficient weight to certain factors and he mentions the personal and family circumstances, good character, voluntary surrender, age, and health, and he paid particular regard to this -- in this morning's submissions to these two latter factors, the age and health. In our response, we can simply rest on our brief, what we said in our response brief. The Trial Chamber did, in fact, consider and did weigh and give weight to these factors. As my colleague Mr. Rodic has mentioned this morning, the Trial Chamber had before it evidence regarding all the physical and also cognitive problems experienced by Mr. Strugar. They were referred to in the Defence final trial closing brief, and that closing brief being referred to in paragraph 467 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. Not only did they have the evidence before it but the Trial Chamber in fact mentioned that it was giving weight to these factors. And if I turn Your Honours' attention my English copy of the judgement to paragraph 469, where the Trial Chamber specifically says: "The accused is 71 years old and in poor health. He suffers, in particular, from some degree of vascular dementia and depression and experiences memory losses." I think that ties into the question asked this morning by His Honour Judge Guney that in fact the Trial Chamber was particularly noting certain features that Mr. Strugar -- that were present in Mr. Strugar's health situation but certainly that does not mean that they disregarded the other evidence regarding what we might call some of the more physical issues experienced by Mr. Strugar. In short, the Defence hasn't shown that the Trial Chamber erred in the exercise of its discretion in having considered and given weight to those factors. This actually concludes my submissions in response the sentence at this stage pending, of course, what I will say this afternoon in our own appeal. And at that point, I will also make comments about the submissions he made regarding the present state of health, or in his words, the deteriorated state of health of Mr. Strugar since the trial and how Your Honours should consider that factor if you come to resentence Mr. Strugar. Thank you. These conclude the submissions of the Prosecution in response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are now going to have a one-hour break. We'll resume at 2.00 p.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Good afternoon. Now, we are going to hear the reply by the Defence. You have half an hour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. In the Prosecution's reply to the Defence appeal, the Prosecution is adamant about its proposition that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj. This theory is supported by the following arguments: They say that the finding of the Chamber was supported by evidence that on the 23rd of November, in Geneva, Kadijevic held negotiations about a cease-fire; on the 5th of December, Jokic was negotiating with the Croatian side; and they also say that Srecko Kovacevic came up with a coordinated attack on the 5th of December. That evening they claim Kovacevic visited Strugar's command. In relation to these arguments, the Defence can say as follows: These are generic statements by the OTP, especially when they say that the finding of the Trial Chamber was supported by evidence. The Defence produced detailed reasons founded on evidence to show that the assumption that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj was entirely unfounded. I will not be repeating those now. The OTP mentioned the negotiations that took place but they appear to show the exact opposite, namely that Strugar did not order the attack on Srdj on the 3rd of December in Belgrade at a meeting with the highest military leaders of the country, was familiarised with the progress of the Geneva negotiations. As a responsible and professional military officer who never ignored any orders or instructions received from his superiors, he stood by the order that he received and the instructions that he received. On the 3rd of December, Strugar attended the meeting in Belgrade and he was told about these facts. He was informed. Jokic, who throughout October, November and December acted as chief negotiator on behalf of the JNA, the army, was informed that he should hold negotiations and sign a cease-fire precisely in keeping with the Geneva Agreement dated the 23rd of November, 1991. However, as the Defence put forward in quite some detail in our brief, the deadline was encroaching for the signing of this agreement and the time was getting shorter and shorter for him. Precisely for what he was adamant throughout November in his combat reports to the 3rd Battalion that was supposed to use its infantry units to take Srdj and which they failed to take. This is why it is important to go back to the arguments put forward by the Defence in our appellate brief, it is important to establish whether Jokic was present in Kupari on the 5th of December. It is important to establish if he was involved in the planning and ordering of this attack. This is not a question that can be allowed to remain open and unresolved, and it is a question of considerable significance for any ruling in this case. The OTP state that on the 5th of December, Kovacevic was in Trebinje. In paragraph 340 of the judgement, the Chamber dealt with this insinuation of an alleged agreement, what is this supposed to mean? Strugar being involved and Kovacevic going to Trebinje but the Trial Chamber dismissed this precisely because there is no evidence to suggest anything in relation to that. This story is based yet again on Jokic's evidence. At 381 of the transcript, or rather 3891 through 3892, Jokic explains precisely this. He explains that the original brigade, the 472nd Brigade to which Captain Kovacevic's battalion belonged was based in Trebinje of all places; its command was based in Trebinje, before the war and during the war. He also says that he often travelled to Trebinje in order to remain in touch with his original brigade. Therefore, this can hardly be used to make insinuations about any contact with Strugar in relation to the attack of the 5th of December. This fact, as I've pointed out already, was known thanks to Jokic's testimony, however Jokic also testified that he was informed about this by two unnamed officers who once worked for that operations group and Kovacevic himself, back in 2001, just before he left for The Hague. So much about the reliability or credibility of his testimony and why does it matter to him even if put like this, he's trying to shift any suspicion of blame from himself, any suspicion that he might have been involved in something that was illicit. Finally, in relation to these arguments put forward by the Prosecution, I would like to remind the Chamber in their analysis of evidence, in their closing arguments and their closing final brief, did not adopt the theory that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj or indeed that this was based on his alleged admission to Colm Doyle to the effect that he had ordered the attack on Dubrovnik. The theory about the attack on Srdj is something that the Prosecution tries to deal with in their reply and tries to support this theory by mentioning the promotion of Captain Kovacevic. They link him to General Strugar. They link this promotion to General Strugar and suggest that this was the reason that he had ordered the attack on Srdj because he was trying to cover up Kovacevic's actions thereby factually condoning his actions although allegedly he had known back in October November 1991 that Kovacevic had been involved in incidents which led to the shelling of the Old Town. They say that Strugar failed to thwart Kovacevic's promotion. In our appellate brief, we address these facts in quite some detail and we also invoke evidence from the trial confirming beyond any doubt at all that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade under the command of Kovacevic in October was not involved in any combat activities when the shelling of the Old Town actually occurred. Further, if we look at the combat orders issued between the 9th and the 13th of November, 1991, by Admiral Jokic, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade and Kovacevic had the following task: They had an axis and they were supposed to use their infantry units to take that axis. However, if you look at these very specific orders, you see that there was no artillery action on the part of the 3rd Battalion. Rather, their brief was quite specific in terms of both time and location. They were to provide support to other artillery units from Jokic's 9th Military Naval Sector. This was not reflected in the transcript. Combat orders between the 3rd -- the 9th and the 13th of November, that Jokic issued were about taking the Srdj elevation. There is also the account provided by Admiral Jokic during his evidence about an alleged investigation that he carried out back in November as to who had been involved in the shelling of Srdj. He claims that he had established at the time that this might have been Captain Kovacevic of which he subsequently informed the 2nd Operations Group requesting his dismissal. But there is evidence disproving these allegations in addition to everything else that the Defence has put forward. Let me just mention one of those. D100, Exhibit D100 in which we see Warship-Captain Zec, the Chief of Staff of the 9th Military Naval Sector on the 26th of November, 1991, making a proposal regarding incentives to members of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Many members of that battalion were nominated for various kinds of promotion, decorations, that sort of thing. This is a proposal. The proposal that he then committed to the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector. This is quite certainly an exhibit that denies any allegations made by Jokic about any investigation that he allegedly conducted back in November 1991, it also shows that no one from another operations group could possibly have known about these actions allegedly taken by Kovacevic. In relation to the promotion procedure under the military rules or if you like, in view of the military reality that prevailed in the JNA, there is one thing that must be pointed out. There were no investigations. There were no insinuations about Kovacevic in relation to the shelling of the Old Town at the time. His proposed promotion dating back to November, because of the JNA procedure and because of the way it worked, proposals are first tabled, they are then considered and so on and so forth. The Supreme Commander of the JNA, Kadijevic, signed this on the 14th of December, signed Kovacevic's promotion which was to be dated the 14th of November, predated, because that's what his merits were about. The promotion was to take effect on the 11th of November because he had distinguished himself in the Srdj action having implemented the orders previously issued by Jokic. Another thing that is significant, by the 14th of December, which is when his fast-track promotion was signed and approved, the Federal Secretary Kadijevic had already received reports forwarded to him by Jokic pursuant to his own order to conduct investigation into the events of the 6th of December and the shelling of the Old Town. What does this mean? Kadijevic is already in possession of Jokic's report in relation to the 6th of December investigation and what exactly went on? Needless to say, these were reports that he forwarded to Kadijevic. And Jokic uses these to explain that Kovacevic launched this attack at his own initiative on that day because he was, at the time, under fire and he was suffering heavy losses due to enemy fire that was emanating from Srdj itself. As for the OTP's allegations about Kadijevic's order to Jokic to conduct an investigation, and about this being no impediment for Strugar to launch a parallel investigation and punish his subordinates, the Defence wishes to say this: In their reply, the OTP have not proposed any arguments to support this claim. Therefore, the Defence believes these to be mere generic allegations. All the more so since, as we know, in the very first report, and now we are discussing the level of information available to Kadijevic or anyone else in possession of this piece of information, even his very first report, Jokic is actually just pretending to be taking measures. As soon as the 7th of December, he is submitting a report to Kadijevic saying that this was an attack launched by Kovacevic of his own accord because he had come under enemy fire, this was not a situation that he could cope with, and he had no choice but to take this measure. As soon as the 7th of December, he submits a report to Kadijevic, as the Supreme Commander, to say that he had replaced Captain Jovanovic who was the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade. The Trial Chamber found that this person could not have been involved in the shelling of the Old Town on the 6th of December. The Prosecutor's reply regarding lack of diligence in Strugar's conduct in preventing or stopping the attack after the telephone call in the morning of the 6th of December from General Kadijevic, this allegation is not consistent with that military reality. Strugar did call Jokic and ordered him to stop the attack. Furthermore, he agreed with the measures that Jokic is informing him of at that moment, that he's sending somebody from the staff, a Colonel from the staff to Zarkovica to stop the attack and so on and so forth. Therefore, Strugar as the superior officer did take sufficient and reasonable measures once he was informed to prevent and to stop the attack. He tells his subordinate officer, a corps commander with a very high rank of General of his orders. He agrees with the measures his subordinate officer tells him he would take, and this is sufficient for Strugar to believe his subordinate officer. I have to go back to Jokic's meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December because it has been mentioned time and time again. I have to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic has no vested interest in establishing the presence or non-presence of Jokic at the Kupari meeting on the 5th of December. Admiral Jokic himself, when testifying before the Trial Chamber, said that he personally led the meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December, 1991. Further in his evidence, Jokic says that he informed his superiors by telephone of his negotiations with the opposing side and he also informed the officers in his staff of the cease-fire that resulted. Thus, Jokic himself states in his evidence that he was in Kupari, that he led the negotiations, he was present at the meeting and when we compare that to Jovanovic's testimony and his reports from 1991, we cannot leave in balance the question of Jokic's presence in Kupari. Regarding the arguments of the Prosecution regarding the status of Mato Valjalo, let me repeat, his duties in the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik can also be viewed in the light of the Law on Defence of the Republic of Croatia because the Crisis Staff in times of war has a military function, participates in the defence of the country in keeping with Croatian legislation. So at that time, Mato Valjalo was mobilised, he was a military conscript. And in keeping with that mobilisation, he was assigned to the duties he was performing at the Crisis Staff. Certainly, after his injury, all that was recognised in the proceedings before the competent authorities of Croatia which granted him the status of military war invalid and we already established that there is another category that of civilian war invalid which is granted to civilians who are injured or wounded during the war. With regard to the Prosecution's reply to the appeal of the Defence concerning sentencing, the Prosecution failed to reply to the arguments of the Defence; namely, in the judgement of the Trial Chamber, only two diseases, two conditions are mentioned. The Defence asserts that at that time, the Trial Chamber had in its possession reports of another five or six conditions which combined make the health of the accused much worse than acknowledged by the Trial Chamber, vascular dementia, depression, and memory loss that were not taken into account. With regard to the same period, the Defence kept the Trial Chamber informed of the deteriorating health as witnessed by appropriate medical reports. And in that way, we informed the Appeals Chamber of this condition, the deteriorating health of Mr. Strugar after the judgement in 2005. We believe all this amounts to and should be treated as a special mitigating circumstance that should be given appropriate weight in sentencing. And precisely in this regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will remind you you still have 4 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will conclude in 30 seconds. I would like to recall, with regard to the sentence and the position of the Prosecution now, that in 2006, the Prosecution withdrew its own appeal precisely for humanitarian reason as stated in the brief which means because of the age and the very poor health of General Strugar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I shall be speaking for myself. At the close of the case, I asked myself whether I have understood the main lines of the argument and here, I must say that I am attracted to your argument which I understand this way that, yes, a commander does have a responsibility to take disciplinary measures against his subordinates, but that in view of the principle of unity of command, that responsibility is as it were, overborne or neutralised by any appropriate action taken at a higher level of command responsibility. But is it allowed in this sense that if the commander is aware that the action purportedly taken at a higher level or in the chain of command is a sham, that neutralisation doesn't apply. What I want to bring to your mind is the sentence which occurs in paragraph 439 of the judgement, it reads: "Rather, the evidence persuades the Chamber the accused was, at the very least, by acquiescence, a participant in the arrangement by which Admiral Jokic undertook his sham investigation and sham disciplinary action." To my mind, the case, in this branch, will turn upon the veracity of that statement: Was that investigation taken at a higher level a sham investigation, and did the accused know that it was a sham? If so, would that neutralise his responsibility to take disciplinary action against his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to paragraph 439 of the judgement that you referred me to, I see that this is a finding of the Trial Chamber. However, what is essential in the view of the Defence is that when the Chamber states that based on the evidence, it is satisfied that the accused, at least on the basis of tacit agreement was a participant in the arrangement by which Admiral Jokic undertook his sham investigation and sham disciplinary action and reported to the 1st Secretariat in a way which deflected responsibility for the damage to the Old Town," in the view of the Defence this is based on conjecture although the word here used is "evidence." However, interestingly enough, there is nothing in the footnote to accompany and corroborate this finding of the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, the question arises -- we understood this part: Kadijevic ordered Jokic to conduct an investigation and report directly to him without anybody interfering. During cross-examination, Admiral Jokic too was asked what I just presented to you as a proposition, whether he copied his reports of the investigation to Strugar. His answer was negative. Everything was directed to Belgrade. There is no evidence that Kadijevic either, once he received all the reports and the videotape of the damage to the Old Town of the 6th December, there is no evidence that Kadijevic shared with Strugar any information concerning responsibility, who organised the attack, who shelled the Old Town, what kind of damage, to what extent was inflicted, what measures were proposed to the Federal Secretary. Neither Jokic nor Kadijevic shared any of this information with Strugar. If, in some way, indirectly he had been informed, that, perhaps, would have constituted grounds for him to inform the Federal Secretary to raise the issue, to ask, perhaps, about the results of the investigation; however, Strugar has no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask this -- exactly the same question put by -- his Learned Judge, Judge Shahabuddeen. But if I can just follow up. Then you would agree with the principle as a matter of law where an investigation ordered by a superior to a commander is a sham, then the commander's duty to investigate and punish would still persist as a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you just make it more specific? I simply don't want to misunderstand this. Which commander are we talking about in this example? Is it Kadijevic-Jokic or Strugar-Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us suppose Mr. Strugar at the time knew that the order to investigate the crimes by General Kadijevic to Jokic was a sham, then Strugar's obligations still persist. Would you agree with that proposition? I'm asking this because probably I take it that you agree with the proposition that an order to commit a crime can be disobeyed, then if an order allows the impunity for a crime, then that kind of order could be disobeyed, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate the logic, the underlying logic in your question. However, what I cannot agree to at all is military reality precisely in the JNA, military doctrine, regulations, and the functioning of that army for 50 or 60 years in the past. It is difficult to assume that when Strugar and Jokic come to report, and when Strugar hears with his very own ears that Kadijevic, as Jokic wrote, was angry, orders Jokic to investigate the matter, to have it done, to have these measures taken, no way could he believe that this is a sham order coming from the Supreme Commander, and given to a high officer, Admiral Jokic. How should I put this? That this is a sham order, a false order to have an investigation carried out. And at that moment, how could the General think that this has to do with a cover-up of a crime? Since that investigation was out of Strugar's jurisdiction, if General Strugar were to become in charge of Jokic again, the investigation and everything else, it is only in that case that one could speak of Strugar's responsibility on the basis of such reports sent by Jokic, whether he looked through them conscientiously enough, whether he paid enough attention to them, and whether he checked the facts contained in these reports. So my answer is that he would have been responsible only if the Supreme Commander would have returned the authority to him to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Just very briefly. In order to add to what I've already said by way of an answer. That is also contrary to the view of the Prosecutor. Let us just look at the logic of all these questions. Shells fell on the old city on the 6th of December. Those shells were fired by soldiers who were manning artillery pieces. According to the then composition, they are commanded by platoon commanders, above them company commanders, above them battalion commanders, then the commander of the 9th VPS Corps and then the commander of the 2nd Operations Group and the Supreme Commander, Kadijevic, above him. Along those lines, where would responsibility stop in terms of who was in charge of taking measures aimed at prevention and punishment? Bearing in mind the specific situation at hand when the superior commander directly assigns a high-ranking officer to investigate and to report to him on the results of the investigation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. The questions that we are now pursuing that my colleagues Judge Shahabuddeen and Kwon asked are of course also relevant to the factual explanations from the Prosecutor. Judge Shahabuddeen, in particular, referred to the problem of -- to the suggestion that the whole set-up was a sham. Now, Judge Kwon pursued that question. I would have liked to hear more argument regarding this -- the quality of that arrangement a sham because it's very, very important, we can just not speculate on that, we would like to hear something more concrete but before giving you the floor, I just wanted to sum up to myself as I see this situation. There was bombardment of Dubrovnik, carried by a unit called 9 VPS. Jokic was a commander of that unit. And Jokic was charged with investigation and reporting. Among the one thing that he did which is, of course, not -- far too mild was that Colonel Jovanovic was removed from his temporary command. Jokic submits a report to Kadijevic and the question then presents itself. Who was the commander who legally bore the duty to investigate, to punish, et cetera, et cetera. The direct commander was Jokic. It was not Strugar who was removed from that. So Strugar was sort of a commander of a commander and I would like later to explain to me why Strugar continued to bear the classical responsibilities of a commander when the unit was under Jokic's command and Jokic was also the investigating and punishing authority. Now, on -- in paragraph 444, the Trial Judgement tells us that "The evidence establishes that the accused, namely Strugar, at all material times had full material and legal authority to act himself, to investigate or to take disciplinary or other adverse action against officers of 9 VPS." There is no footnote here and I would like to know what is the evidence on which this statement rests. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second Operations Group that was headed by General Strugar is a temporary military unit which was set up ad hoc consisting of several units, several corps. The 9th military sector is excluded from the army district that was called the Military Naval District that is to say the entire navy. The corps of Admiral Jokic was excluded from that. The fact that this corps then was placed under the operative control of the 2nd Operative Group remains. Then there is the Uzice Corps and there were several other formations that were changed in the meantime. This sentence from paragraph 444 that you read out, pertains to the usual state of affairs, if I can put it that way. That is to say that the state of affairs that is in keeping with military regulations, namely that within the 2nd Operation Group which is at army rank, you have the 9th Military Naval Sector whose commander is Admiral Jokic, then you also have a brigade whose commander is I don't know, somebody else, and you have yet another corps that has its own commander. Again, a higher-ranking officer. These are Strugar's subordinate commanders. They report to him regularly about the activities of their units, and they propose measures to resolve problems in the field, in the area that they are in charge of in terms of their area of responsibility from a military and territorial point of view. Their proposals are discussed in the staff of the 2nd Operations Group. They are either accepted or rejected, amended, then certain orders are passed and then they are passed further down to the subordinate commands of the corps including the 9th VPS and Admiral Jokic. From that point of view, when the Trial Chamber says that from that aspect, the accused had full material and legal authority to act himself, or rather to command his subordinates to take measures to investigate or take disciplinary or other adverse action against the officers of the 9th VPS, this presupposes a procedure of a disciplinary investigation that can be ordered by General Strugar to his subordinates. However, what we have here is an exceptional situation, not a regular situation, the usual type of situation. Again, on the basis of laws and regulations, these are exceptional situations. When the supreme military minister gives an order two steps down or even three steps down and when he asks Jokic directly to do something because the supreme minister realises that Strugar is commander of a temporary formation set up ad hoc for that particular occasion or rather in that particular situation in the then Yugoslavia, that this military naval sector is a unit that has Dubrovnik under its authority for the past 50 years and that Jokic was commander of that military and naval sector for 10 years and he was fully familiar with the area from beforehand. He knew everything in the area. Therefore, it was logical, as the Trial Chamber establishes then, that Kadijevic orders Jokic to carry out the investigation because Jokic is the one who can carry it out in the fastest and most efficient and best way. So this is an exceptional situation. May I just add one thing, just one sentence? I do beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, sir, because we have overstepped the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm about to finish. Since the Judge's question was: Who was the officer that had the mandate to punish? According to this order, Jokic could mete out punishment himself and Kadijevic on the basis of these reports, he could instruct Jokic how to punish and Kadijevic himself could have punished on the basis of the reports of the investigation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to give the floor to the Prosecution for their submissions on their own appeal, apparently we should have a break around quarter to 4.00. Is that feasible? In principle you have 45 minutes. If you can finish any earlier, we might catch up with the time we have lost in relation to the scheduling order. You need how many minutes or how much time, Ms. Brady?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the entirety of the Prosecution appeal, we believe that we will need about one hour and ten minutes. We have one hour and a half according to the Scheduling Order. We don't think we'll go as long as that, though at the same time, I'm going to provide some further amplification on some of the questions that were posed especially this morning and this afternoon by Their Honours Judges Meron and Judge Shahabuddeen. We think we can do whole of the Prosecution and those question in one hour and 10, 15 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may not have quite understood. We must have a break. You are entitled to an hour and a half. We must make a technical break, as it were. That's why I raised the issue with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. What I will -- what I intend to do is start by giving some clarification to some of the questions that were answered this morning by my colleague, Mr. Tracol and also just a few comments in relation to the questions which Judge Meron and other members of the Bench asked this afternoon. Then we will move to the first ground of appeal. I believe we can do that all in 45 minutes and then I will turn to the sentence appeal that we have in the remaining time and it should be no more than about 20 minutes on that. As I mentioned, Your Honours, I will clarify some aspects to answers that were given this morning by my colleague Mr. Tracol and in particular, it came up again in relation to a question asked by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen this afternoon to the Defence. I'm not quoting your question but to paraphrase it, His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen asked a question to the effect that: If the order that came from above, if the order from Kadijevic was also one which was designed to conceal the real events on the day, whether we call it a sham or at least one which was designed to present a certain version of events, as I understood the question, His Honour asked: Can this let those below, the other subordinates down in the chain who also have their own duties to investigate, can it let them off the hook? Our answer to this is a clear no. It cannot let them off the hook. Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen pointed to paragraph 439 of the judgement. In addition to that, Your Honours, I'd point you to paragraph 442 of the judgement. Now, in that part of the judgement, the Chamber repeats that it's not satisfied that General Strugar was excluded and then it says at the end of paragraph 442: "Rather, the Chamber finds he was at least prepared to accept a situation in which he would not become directly involved leaving all effective investigation, action and decisions concerning disciplinary or other adverse action to his immediate subordinate, Admiral Jokic." These are the very important words, "Whose task effectively was known to the accused to be to smooth over the events of 6 December 1991 as best he could with both the Croatian and ECMM interests while providing a basis on which it could be maintained by the JNA that it had taken appropriate measures." In other words, Your Honours, and also I point to other parts of the judgement, paragraph 435, in essence, the JNA at this point was in what we might call colloquially damage control mode. And Strugar was aware that this was a damage control, it was -- it could also be called a PR, public relations exercise. If Your Honours's proposition ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do you have a problem, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing, if you could please explain this. I'm not sure if this is because of what the Prosecutor seems to be saying now, but are we now reopening, in a manner of speaking, a new ground of responses and replies? Because I think the Prosecutor is now responding to our reply. Is this a procedure that is established before the Trial Chamber? What I was thinking was the idea that I had was that there was no further response to our reply. In other words, will I be given a chance to reply yet again to what the Prosecutor seems to be saying now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the Judges have conferred. The Judges put their own question, therefore it is quite normal that Ms. Brady be entitled to respond. What we are going to be asking her is to respond briefly to the questions put by the Bench and then to address the Prosecution's appeal. If, in addition, you have anything to add, you must make it very short because we have already spent a lot of time on these issues. Ms. Brady, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will endeavour to speak only to the questions that were raised and to assist on these points. As I was saying, in further response to the question posed by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, essentially if the proposition was allowed, was to be accepted that once an order comes from above, that is designed to conceal or to present a sham, then all others are off the hook. This would mean from top to bottom, there would be an exoneration of people on their duty to investigate and take proper steps and this, of course, would not be acceptable. I can also point Your Honours to the testimony of Admiral Jokic who, on the way back on travelling back from Belgrade from the meeting with Kadijevic, as they're travelling back, he talks to Strugar on the way back and Your Honours, at transcript page -- transcript 29th of March, 2004, transcript reference is 4086 to 87. This is what Jokic said about that conversation with Strugar on the way back from Belgrade. And I'm quoting from the transcript: Jokic said, "It was accepted that the official version of the events of the 6th of December which was composed at the command of the 2nd Operational Group on the basis of information provided by Captain Kovacevic which was given by his officers, that this official version of the event should be sent to Belgrade to the General Staff and that I should stand by that story, that version at the press conference on the following day." So Strugar well knew what exactly the investigation would entail. In brief answer to Judge Meron's question about whether General Strugar could have asked to see the report prepared by Jokic, so even if he had understood the situation was that Kadijevic gave an order directly to Jokic, what stopped him, as it were, from asking to see the report? Our answer to that is yes. Yes, of course he could get the report. It would actually be inconceivable under normal military doctrine if he could not, and especially in a -- in the JNA command system where you have this two up, two down doctrine which expert Zorc spoke about which emphasised that a duty of a commander is to be informed two levels up and two levels down. I also stress that another important factor that at some stage as commander he would have had to have found out about the results of that report so he could take necessary and reasonable measures. The simple reason being that it was directly about troops under his command. Your Honour Judge Meron also had a concern arising from this morning's questioning about the finding in paragraph 445 of the judgement. This finding, if I could summarize the essence of this finding, it's basically this: That even if Strugar understood at that time that he was out of the loop, the Trial Chamber finds he still should have done something. I think Judge Meron was troubled by this because it seemed that -- at first blush it could seem to be going too far to expect General Strugar to defy his boss, the Supreme Command, General Kadijevic and his order. Except I think you have to keep one thing in mind and you have to keep coming back to the purpose of the exercise. And again come back to the paragraph 444. The purpose was to present a certain version which would basically sit with the Croatians, sit with the ECMM, the international monitors, and then also allow things to look as if the JNA had taken measures. Again, a PR exercise. The Trial Chamber in that paragraph also notes that Strugar could have resigned and yet he did not. At the end of the day, as my colleague Mr. Tracol did emphasise, no one was punished by the removal of one person, Mr. Jovanovic who was simply removed from his one day temporary assignment as battalion commander of the 5th Brigade and he wasn't -- his units weren't actually even directly involved on the day of the shelling. So at the end of the day, the one person who was identified by the investigation, that is, Kovacevic, the one person who was identified as directly involved, far from being punished, he was promoted. That speaks volumes about General Strugar's acquiescence in the situation. My last point. I'd like to deal with Judge Meron's question relating to paragraph 444 and in particular, Your Honour's concern about the finding on whether or not the accused at all material times had full material and legal authority to act himself to investigate or take disciplinary or other adverse action against these troops who directly participated. Your Honour noted that, and correctly so, that there is no footnote to that finding. However, the findings were already made by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 412 to 413 of the judgement. If I could take Your Honours to those paragraphs. In 412, the Trial Chamber found that: "As the commander of the 2 OG, the accused could also ensure the replacement of a subordinate commander during combat operations by recommending to the federal secretary of national defence the removal of the officer supported by an explanation." And there there's a reference in the footnote 1195 to Exhibit P204, and to the testimony of Admiral Jokic at transcript page 3906. General Jokic said at 3906 about this very matter as to whether or not Strugar would have had the legal and full material ability to take action, as it were, against these people at this stage, he said: "Well, according to the law, the commander of the operational group held the rank of army commanders. He could have suspended or replaced a subordinate commander, anybody. That's the kind of authority he had. He had the right to replace anyone in any subordinate command." Your Honours, that completes our further answer in -- further articulation of Your Honours' questions. I would now turn the podium over to my colleague, Ms. Jarvis who will address you on the Prosecution's first ground of appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution's first ground of appeal can be summarized in simple terms. The Trial Chamber found that General Strugar's duty to prevent the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik was triggered at around 7.00 in the morning of 6 December by which time he had been telephoned by General Kadijevic in Belgrade and put on notice that the shelling of the Old Town was then already underway. The Trial Chamber also found that even prior to that time, based on the prevailing circumstances, General Strugar also had notice of a real and obvious risk that the shelling would take place. But the Chamber found that he was not legally obliged to do anything about it at that earlier point in time. We submit that that was wrong, that it's antithetical to the notion of responsible command that underpins superior responsibility, and that it would, in large part, render meaningless a superior's duty to prevent future crimes. My submissions today are divided into four parts. In the first part, I'll explain to you why this ground of appeal matters. Why is it so important to recognise that Strugar's duty to prevent the crimes preceded the time when he received the phone call from Kadijevic. In part two, I'll explain in more detail the factual backdrop in which this issue arises in the present case. In part 3, I'll explain the nature of the Trial Chamber's error and why the Trial Chamber was wrong to find that the mens rea standard for Article 7(3) is not met based on a real and obvious risk of future crimes. In part 4, I'll explain what the outcome in this case should have been had the correct standard been applied. Turning then to the first part. Why is it so important for the Appeals Chamber to confirm that Strugar's duties as a commander to prevent the shelling preceded General Kadijevic's phone call and within the confines of the indictment in this case, extended back to midnight on 6 December 1991. It matters because it represents the difference between, on the one hand, requiring that Strugar control a real and obvious risk of shelling to ensure that the shelling of the Old Town never started, and on the other hand, requiring only that he intervene once he's on notice that damage to life and property is already happening. Let's not forget what was at stake in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. As the Trial Chamber specifically noted at paragraph 285, on 6 December, the Old Town was unique and irreplaceable not just because it was a UNESCO World Heritage protected site but because it was a living city with a resident population of about 7.000 to 8.000 people. When the JNA artillery turned on the Old Town on 6 December, two people were killed and two were seriously injured. If Strugar had intervened to control the obviously risky situation developing within his units, those victims might have been spared. One of the victims was Tonci Skocko, a young man of about 19 who was killed very early in the attack at about 8.00 in the morning. Witness Nikola Jovic recounted counted for the Trial Chamber how when Tonci was hit by shrapnel, his father Mato risked his life going outside the Old Town to get his car to race his son to hospital. He said, "At the moment when Mato returned, he drove his car through the Skalina, the streets, actually the stairs, the steps and his tyres were totally deflated so that he actually drove on the tyre rims." Jovic continued, "Well, you can imagine a person ... who saw this happening to his own son. You can imagine what kind of a reaction he had. The demeanour of his father is something that's hard to describe. It is the demeanour of a father whose son is dying in his arms." That's at transcript 2944 to 2945. Similarly, if Strugar had intervened to prevent the shelling ever getting underway, the damage caused to the buildings of the Old Town on 6 December might have been averted. ECMM representative Per Hvalkof described the Old Town in the wake of the 6 December attack as looking like "a missile garbage lot." That's at trial judgement paragraph 316. This description is visually confirmed by a film of the Old Town taken during and after the 6 December attack and I'm going to play some very brief excerpts from that film for you now. And this was Exhibit P66 at trial and the excerpts are taken at time markers 32 minutes 15 seconds to 28 seconds, and 34 minutes 51 seconds to 37 minutes. And the latter is cited in the trial judgement at footnote 971.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: As witness Fietelaars, former Netherlands ambassador to the Yugoslavia put it, this damage done to the Old Town was "not only Croatia's problem; it's a problem of the whole world. It's not only that within UNESCO the status of Dubrovnik was particularly pointed out as a city of major importance of the human cultural heritage but also that something that has played such a central role in European history for almost 1.000 years should not be touched like that and it should not be destroyed." That's at transcript 4315. The Trial Chamber in the Jokic sentencing judgement at paragraph 52 underscored this point, emphasising that once damage is done to buildings like this, they can never be restored to their original state. The Prosecution's first ground of appeal, then, is not just about extending Strugar's duty to prevent by a further seven hours. It's about Strugar's duty as a commander to ensure that the shelling of the Old Town never started and that no life and no part of the irreplaceable heritage of humankind were lost. This brings me to part 2 of my submissions which is to explain in more detail the factual backdrop to this issue. Even before Kadijevic's phone call to Strugar on the morning of 6 December, Strugar was on notice of a risky situation that could escalate to the point where the Old Town of Dubrovnik was shelled. Consider, Your Honours, the situation confronting Strugar on the eve of the Srdj attack. Strugar was the commander of JNA units who had been involved in a military campaign in the confined geographic region of Dubrovnik since October 1991. He knew that during combat operations in October, his forces had shelled the Old Town of Dubrovnik. This shelling caused damage to several buildings. Strugar knew that his forces had again shelled the Old Town during combat operations between 10 and 13 November. The Trial Chamber, in particular, accepted that evidence that on the 12th of November, the shelling of the Old Town had been deliberate and sustained. Strugar knew that the October and November shelling was not the result of isolated or uncharacteristic behaviour within his units. Rather, it was symptomatic of a pervasive lack of discipline. The evidence revealed general problems within Strugar's units of unauthorised weapons fire, refusal to carry out orders, looting, arson, and drinking. Strugar knew that the October and November shelling occurred in the course of attacks in which the JNA were seeking to capture territory in the vicinity of Dubrovnik including in November, the very same location being sought on 6 of December, Srdj. He knew that existing orders prohibiting attacks on cultural property and the Old Town had been ineffective in October and November. He knew that he had not taken any steps to punish the perpetrators of the previous shelling. As the Trial Chamber put it at paragraph 415 and this should appear on your screens, Your Honours: "There had been no example of adverse disciplinary or other consequences shown to those who breached the existing orders, or international law on previous occasions." Strugar knew that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade was implicated in the November shelling and that he had ordered them into combat again on 6 December still under the same commander, Kovacevic, whose nickname was Rambo. He knew this battalion was still equipped with substantial artillery just as they had been in November. And Strugar also knew that the order to attack Srdj involved the prospect that his forces might well have the need to shell wider positions in Dubrovnik and that the plan for the attack on Srdj provided for the use of "quite a formidable artillery capacity," most of which was capable of firing at the Old Town. That's paragraph 91 and 343 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber accepted all of these factors and it specifically found at paragraph 417 of the judgement that based on all of these factors, even before he received the phone call from Kadijevic, Strugar knew of, and again, the quote will appear on your screens: " ... a real and obvious prospect, a clear possibility, that in the heat and emotion of the attack on Srdj, the artillery under his command might well get out of hand once again and commit offences of the type charged." In the Chamber's view, "This was a risk that was not slight or remote." The Chamber at paragraph 420 fully accepted that this risk was, and the quote is on your screens, "Sufficiently real and the consequences of further undisciplined and illegal shelling so potentially serious that a cautious commander may well have thought it desirable to make it explicitly clear that the order to attack Srdj did not include authority to supporting artillery to shell, at the least, the Old Town." But the Chamber found that a superior like Strugar, who is on notice of such a real and obvious risk is not required to do anything. We submit that was wrong and that at that point, Strugar was obliged to control the situation and take preventative steps. This brings me to part 3 of my submissions concerning the Trial Chamber's erroneous finding that Article 7(3) mens rea standard is not met based on proof of a real and obvious risk of future crimes. The Trial Chamber does not clearly state in the judgement why it considers that, as a matter of law, a real and obvious risk of future crimes is insufficient to trigger a superior's duty to prevent. But there are strong indications in the judgement that the Chamber conceptualised a superior's duty to prevent as limited to situations where crimes are either already underway or there is a definite plan by subordinates to commit crimes which could have been discovered if investigation had been carried out. This is particularly evident at paragraph 416 where the Chamber considers that a superior who is on notice of a risk of crimes must, and the quote is on your screens, "At least investigate i.e., take steps inter alia to determine whether in truth offences are about to be committed, or indeed by that stage have been committed or are being committed." This particular lens for viewing superior responsibility is reflected again in paragraph 417 of the judgement where the Chamber points out that: "This is not shown to be a case, for example, where the accused had information that before the attack, his forces planned or intended to shell the Old Town unlawfully, or the like. It is not apparent that any additional investigation would have put the accused in any better position." We submit, Your Honours, that this approach cannot be correct because it leaves entirely unregulated situations where there is an obvious risk that spontaneous or opportunistic crimes may be committed in the future. Let me give you an example to explain what I mean. Consider, Your Honours, the situation of a superior who knows that previously, troops in one of his units who were stationed in a village were drinking heavily, got drunk, and then massacred civilians. These troops were never punished and were then moved to another village. This superior then finds out that troops from this unit have been drinking heavily again. What does the law require of a superior in this kind of situation? It must be that a superior, knowing of such a real and obvious risk that crimes will be repeated against civilians must intervene to diffuse the situation. For example, by immediately removing the troops or sending in reinforcements to keep the troops under control. An investigation by a superior at this point would not reveal that crimes were pre-planned, but it would be an entirely unsatisfactory outcome if this superior was allowed to do nothing until civilians were actually being massacred. We say the situation confronting Your Honours here is similar. In our brief and our supplementary filing of 1 October 2007, we have set out extensive argument explaining why the Trial Chamber's approach is contrary to the case law of this Tribunal, World War II case law, state practice, and the rationale underpinning the superior responsibility doctrine. Today all I want to do is highlight two cases before this Tribunal that show the Trial Chamber's approach in the present case was in error. The first of those is the Krnojelac appeal judgement. Your Honours, the language used by the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber confirms that a real and obvious risk of future crimes is sufficient to trigger a superior's duty to prevent. The language is set out in full in our brief at paragraph 2.26, but in essence, the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber accepted that a superior who is on notice of a risk of crimes or that crimes might subsequently be committed must take steps to prevent those crimes. The factual analysis in Krnojelac, particularly on the crime of torture is instructive. The Krnojelac Trial Chamber had found that the fact Krnojelac witnessed the torture of one particular detainee in the KP Dom prison, a person called Zekovic, was not of itself sufficient to trigger Krnojelac's duty to prevent the recurrence of such tortures in the future. The Appeals Chamber specifically overturned this finding at paragraph 169 and the quote will appear on your screens. "The Appeals Chamber does not share the Trial Chamber's opinion that the fact that the accused witnessed the beating of Zekovic, ostensibly for the prohibited purpose of punishing him for his failed escape is not sufficient, in itself, to conclude that the accused knew or had reason to know that other than in that particular instance, beatings were inflicted for any of the prohibited purposes." Importantly, the Appeals Chamber found that based on Zekovic's torture, in the context of the prevailing circumstances of the KP Dom prison at the time, Krnojelac had reason to know that his subordinates might commit other acts of torture in the future and held him responsible for failing to prevent those future crimes. Again, Your Honours, this was not a case where any investigation carried out by Krnojelac after witnessing Zekovic's torture would have necessarily revealed a plan to commit future tortures. But nevertheless, Krnojelac was considered to be on notice of future crimes and held responsible for failing to prevent. The second case I want to refer to is the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement which was rendered yesterday. And this judgement supports the Prosecution's appeal in the present case. I have five brief points that I want to make in relation to this case. First of all, the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement at paragraph 31 confirms that the relevant mens rea threshold for Article 7(3) is notice of a risk of crimes or that crimes might be committed in the future. We say this accords with the Krnojelac appeal judgement which used the very same language. The Appeals Chamber has therefore accepted that a superior who is on notice of a possibility of future crimes has reason to know within the meaning of Article 7(3). This is also consistent with the Delalic appeal judgement at paragraph 238 which states that, "a showing that a superior had some general information in his possession, which would put him on notice of possible crimes -- possible unlawful acts by his subordinates would be sufficient to prove he had reason to know." Certainly, Your Honours, the Prosecution does not suggest that notice of a slight or remote possibility would be sufficient to incur criminal liability but Strugar, having reason to know of a real and obvious risk of the shelling of the Old Town must fall within the threshold that has been articulated by the Appeals Chamber. Secondly, the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber expressly accepted that a superior's knowledge of and failure to punish past crimes is relevant in assessing the risk of future crimes. For example, at paragraphs 30 and 267. The third point is that the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber emphasised that the assessment of risk must be done in light of the specific circumstances of each case. There is no automatic formula for proving that a superior has reason to know. That's at paragraph 31. I submit that what this means is that when it comes to notice based on past criminal conduct, those crimes must be committed in circumstances alerting a superior to the real possibility that they might be repeated again in the future. For all the reasons I've given in the beginning of my submissions today, this is such a case. We are dealing here with a repeated pattern of past crimes which went unpunished and in light of pervasive disciplinary problems and all the other contextual factors that I've mentioned. The fourth point from Hadzihasanovic is that the Appeals Chamber's application of the law to the facts underscores the validity of the Prosecution's appeal in this case. In particular, concerning detention crimes in Bugojno, the Appeals Chamber overturned the Trial Chamber's finding that Hadzihasanovic failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the crimes at the furniture salon which was the trigger for his duty to prevent subsequent crimes. It's a very different situation to the present case where Strugar took no steps in respect of the prior shelling of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: And the risk of future crimes was further heightened by the series of other factors that I've mentioned.
