Concerning the plunder in Vares, the Appeals Chamber overturned the finding that Kubura had reason to know of plunder in Vares just because he knew that plunder had previously been committed in Ovnak some five months earlier and 40 kilometres removed. But again, contrast that to the situation here where the mid-November shelling of the Old Town occurred just a few weeks before the same conduct was repeated in exactly the same place on 6 December. My fifth and final point from Hadzihasanovic is that the Appeals Chamber stated that a superior who is on notice of a risk that crimes might happen in the future is required to investigate further. This is an important point, Your Honour, and we submit that this should not be understood as a statement that a superior's duty to prevent only applies where an investigation would have revealed with certainty that the crimes were planned or already underway. We submit that the Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic did not intend to exclude situations where a superior knows spontaneous or opportunistic crimes might occur. Your Honours, the Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber in this case clarify that a superior who has notice of a real possibility of future crimes is required not only to investigate but to take the necessary preventative steps to address the known risk and, in addition, that if a superior fails to do so, criminal -- and the crimes subsequently occur, criminal liability will result. This brings me to the final part of my submissions and I can be very brief so as to conclude before the break. Accepting that even prior to Kadijevic's phone call, Strugar had a duty to take preventative measures, what should be the outcome in this case? I submit that that question is easily answered on the facts as found in the trial judgement. At paragraph 421, the Trial Chamber expressly found that when issuing his order to attack Srdj, Strugar could have, but did not, specifically clarify that the Old Town must not be shelled. That, of itself, is sufficient to show that Strugar failed in his duties as a commander to prevent the crimes prior to 7.00 a.m. on 6 December. In our brief, we've also outlined other necessary and reasonable preventative measures that were argued at trial that Strugar could have also taken. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions and I would be happy to assist with questions if you have any at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions. We are going to have a 20-minute break. We will resume at five past 4.00. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I see -- I believe that Judge Kwon wants to put a question to Ms. Jarvis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President. Ms. Jarvis, I have been interested in the issue of notice of risk that would sufficiently trigger the superior's obligation pursuant to 7(3). I understand that the Prosecution's argument in this case is that the fact in this case may well fall within the sphere of higher standard. However, the standard you put forward seems to be a bit lower one. For example, I can refer to the -- your appeal brief, page 11, paragraph 225 where you say: "Notice of risk of criminal conduct is sufficient to trigger a superior's duty under Article 7(3) insofar as for mens rea." When I read this paragraph, I was wondering what degree of risk you would mean and whether we could -- we would be able to formulate a workable standard in practice. However, I noted and I was pleased to hear that you submitted a few minutes ago that "the Prosecution does not suggest that notice of a slight or removed possibility will be sufficient to incur criminal liability but Strugar having reason to know of a real and obvious risk of the shelling of the Old Town must fall within the threshold that has been articulated by the Appeals Chamber." I also remember in Krnojelac and the -- which is also cited Hadzihasanovic recently, referred to sufficiently alarming informations. And I also remember Ms. Baig referring to real and unreasonable notice this morning, although the transcript reads real and reasonable. So you would agree with the qualifying adjective, the real and obvious, that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can perhaps begin my response by saying that as I've mentioned, the language of the Appeals Chamber to date in cases like Krnojelac and more recently Hadzihasanovic has specified that a risk or the possibility that crimes might happen in the future will trigger a superior's duty under Article 7(3) so that's as much clarification as we have in the case law at the moment, so that's the basis for our submission. I have said in my submission today that we interpret this language, and particularly the use of the word "might" by both the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber and the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber as confirming that a possibility of future crimes is sufficient and I've mentioned that language is consistent with the Delalic Appeals Chamber on this point as well. But as I also said, a possibility is a broad term and there can certainly be high possibilities and lower possibilities and we certainly don't suggest that a low possibility would be appropriate, that it must be, as Your Honour has said, something alarming enough to propel the superior into action to take preventative steps. The reason why we've brought this ground of appeal in this very case is precisely because the Chamber's language indicates it was a real and obvious risk and it is problematic to suggest that a superior who is on notice of that kind of a risk, that degree of risk is not required to do anything and we say that's inconsistent with previous case law. Your Honours also referred to the formulation of a real and reasonable risk or a real and reasonably foreseeable risk and Your Honours, that language was used by the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber. They considered this precise issue and they looked at the Strugar trial judgement and said, we don't agree with that kind of approach because we think effectively that means a superior doesn't have to do anything until crimes are already happening; that can't be right. We of course agree with that. It's the very position that we're running in this case. This formulation of a real and reasonably foreseeable risk, we say, is an appropriate one and we see it as essentially the same as a real and obvious risk which is what the Trial Chamber has used in the present case. We say that those are all acceptable formulations and fit within the Tribunal's existing case law. But certainly, Your Honours, this would be a juncture at which, if the Appeals Chamber was to clarify the risk standard that is applicable, that would be of great assistance for future cases and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal more generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you go for real and present danger?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I missed the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you go for real and present danger?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, we submit that that kind of language is around the mark of what we're talking about and that it actually accords with another formulation of the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber. Throughout the judgement, they use slightly different formulations and one of the formulations is actually a real and present risk. And we submit that they all amount to the same thing. And Your Honour Judge Kwon is right to say what you are looking for is a situation where there is sufficiently alarming information to require a superior to act. A real and present danger, a real and obvious risk, a real and reasonably foreseeable risk, we say, that's what we're looking for in these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution still has the floor for the remainder of its submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll now turn to the Prosecution's third ground of appeal on the sentence. Your Honours are aware of the findings in this case which have been -- many of which have been highlighted during this appeals hearing. In essence, General Strugar stands convicted under Article 7(3) for failing to prevent and failing to punish the deliberate and indiscriminate shelling of the World Heritage listed Old Town of Dubrovnik by forces under his command. And as we've seen in Ms. Jarvis's presentation, the shelling led to extensive damage to civilian and cultural property, as well as civilian deaths and injuries. In our submission, the eight-year sentence that he received is manifestly inadequate and should be increased. Our detailed arguments are set out in our appeal brief so today I will merely highlight two main points. First, the Trial Chamber's erroneous comparison of Strugar's case with Jokic's case which contributed to the Trial Chamber's selection of a too lenient sentence for Mr. Strugar. And in this, I will be focussing on two sets of -- two key sets of differences between the two accused. Firstly, their respective levels of authority in the command structure, and their roles on the day of the shelling; and secondly, differences arising from Jokic's plea of guilt and his substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. The second point I'll be highlighting today concerns the Trial Chamber's error in having regarded the statement which Strugar made at the end of his trial as one of remorse and according it weight in mitigation. I'll turn now to the main thrust of our appeal and that is the Trial Chamber's comparison with Jokic's sentence. Just to briefly recap: Admiral Jokic pleaded guilty and was convicted under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting the units responsible for the shelling of the Old Town, and Article 7(3) for failing to prevent and punish their crimes. He was sentenced to seven years by the Trial Chamber. On appeal, the Appeals Chamber upheld his Article 7(1) conviction for aiding and abetting, vacated his Article 7(3) conviction in light of his Article 7(1) conviction, and affirmed his seven-year sentence. Now, we say that the Strugar Trial Chamber was not wrong to use Jokic's 7-year sentence as a reference point, as a comparative reference point. Both accused were convicted for essentially the same crimes arising from the shelling of the Old Town and for essentially the same criminal conduct. Jokic for aiding an abetting which was based on his failure to prevent them. And Strugar for failing to prevent and punish the crimes. But there are significant differences between the two accused. Where the Trial Chamber erred was by not considering or not properly considering these significant differences which should have led to a far greater divergence in their sentences than merely the one year that presently separates them. As I mentioned, the two main ones being their relative levels of authority in the JNA command structure and their roles on the day of the shelling; and secondly, the set of circumstances arising from Jokic's plea and cooperation. Turning first to their relative levels in the command structure and their roles that day and this corresponds to our first sub-ground in this ground of appeal. The Trial Chamber was wrong in paragraph 464 in treating Strugar and deeming that Strugar was "more remotely responsible" than Jokic, the immediate and direct commander of the forces involved in the shelling. It goes without saying from what I'm about to say that we disagree with the Defence's arguments which have been put in their briefs about the respective differences in their levels and their roles. Although they held equivalent military ranks, at the time of the operations, General Strugar was hierarchically senior to Admiral Jokic in the JNA military chain of command. This difference in hierarchy was very significant. We mustn't forget, Strugar was the most senior operational commander in the area at that time. All forces in the area operated under his command. In our submission, this position, or rather, this level of authority makes him more responsible and not as the Trial Chamber found less so. Why do we say this? As it was stressed in yesterday's Appeals Judgement in the Hadzihasanovic case, a high level of authority does not necessarily attract greater responsibility. A position or a level of authority does not per se lead to increased responsibility. But, as that judgement, the Hadzihasanovic judgement recognises, in paragraph 320, the superior's abuse of that level of authority can be taken into consideration. We of course recognise that gradation of sentences based on seniority is not an absolute principle, but in this case it is warranted. Why? Strugar's more senior level in the JNA military chain of command necessarily entrusted upon him more responsibilities. He was an army corps commander. By failing to properly perform those heightened responsibilities, his abuse of authority, his very senior level of authority can be said to be greater than Jokic's. His higher level of command authority also meant that when he abused that authority, this had more far-reaching consequences. In a military command structure, one which is based on orders which must be followed, as a commander grows in seniority, the number of units under him who may not perform as they should, and be encouraged by failures and inaction to not perform as they should grow exponentially. But it's not just that Strugar was in charge, in overall charge of the units. In many ways, factually, at the time, at the relevant time, General Strugar had more control over the perpetrators of the crimes that day and more ability to prevent their crimes than did Jokic. It's true, we take no issue with the fact that Jokic was the immediate commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade and the other 9 VPS units involved that day and we agree that at least in the morning hours of that day, Jokic was somewhat geographically closer to Zarkovica and Dubrovnik. But it was Strugar who the Trial Chamber found ordered the attack on Srdj, not Jokic. And it was Strugar who could order Jokic, not the other way around. Strugar, in fact, had a greater ability to control the units that day and to ensure such crimes did not continue once he was upon notice of them. On the Trial Chamber's findings, he took no steps or at best wholly ineffective ones. So that's our first point, that the Trial Chamber was wrong to characterise Strugar as more remotely responsible than Jokic when sentencing him. I'll turn now to the second set of key differences between the Strugar and Jokic cases which the Trial Chamber also paid insufficient regard to when sentencing Strugar. This corresponds to the third sub-ground of this ground of appeal. It boils down to this: Jokic pleaded guilty. Jokic cooperated substantially with the Prosecution, testifying as a key witness in this case and in fact, the Jokic Trial Chamber called Jokic's plea and cooperation when they were sentencing Jokic, "exceptionally important," exceptionally important mitigating factors. That's at the Jokic sentencing appeal judgement, paragraph 114. And yet, even though the Strugar Trial Chamber mentioned the plea of guilt from Jokic, it failed to even mention the significance that Jokic's cooperation would have had on the Jokic Trial Chamber's choice of a seven-year sentence. These key mitigating factors in Jokic's case which the Trial Chamber used to significantly decrease his sentence, the plea of guilt, the cooperation, are simply not present in Strugar's case. And the one year difference in their sentences, seven years for Jokic, eight years for Strugar, fails to reflect this, particularly -- particularly when we bear in mind what I've already said about their levels of authority and their roles. Before I turn to our final point concerning remorse, and this would be a convenient point in which I will make a few remarks on the Defence's argument that Jokic is in fact more criminally responsible than Strugar. He's made them in the briefs both in support of his own appeal and in response to ours. He basically argues Jokic was convicted of six counts, Strugar only two. He mentions the more property damage which Jokic pleaded to and the fact that Jokic was convicted under Article 7(1) for aiding and abetting which they allege is a more direct form of liability. None of these arguments have merit. The gravaman of the crimes -- the gravaman of the crimes of Strugar and Jokic are essentially the same and the fact that Jokic was cumulatively convicted of six offences to which he pled guilty and Strugar only two arising out of the same criminal activity doesn't change that. Nor does the somewhat wide of scope of damage that Jokic pleaded to. Just because Jokic was convicted under Article 7(1) does not make this more -- does not per se make this more serious. As a matter of law, Article 7(3) crimes are not inherently less serious than Article 7(1) crimes and especially when, as here, the basis for Jokic's aiding and abetting conviction is precisely because he failed in his duty as a superior that day and thus to prevent the crimes. We have, in effect, different labels but the same essential criminality. I will now turn to our final point which is that the Trial Chamber erred in treating the statement made by Strugar at the end of his trial as sincere remorse is sufficient to qualify as a mitigating factor. This is the error in paragraphs 470 and 471 and this is our -- corresponds to our second sub-ground of appeal in this ground of appeal. In making this submissions, we recognise that the Trial Chamber may only have given limited weight in mitigation to this factor, to this statement. However, in our submission, having given it any credit was wrong. Remorse is -- by it's very nature, a subjective experience. It can only -- its presence can only be established by either the words used or by being backed up with objective criteria, objective indicia. But in this case, if you look at General Strugar's statement, the one that he gave at the end of the trial, he gave what could only be called a generalized apology for the harms of war. He denied any personal wrongdoing or responsibility. He even failed to acknowledge that crimes occurred. In our submission, this sort of statement simply cannot qualify as remorse sufficient to be a mitigating factor in sentence. I invite Your Honours to compare Strugar 's statement that he gave at the end of the trial with the qualitatively different situation of sincere remorse expressed in the Jokic case. In the briefs, the Defence has tried to compare the statements made by Jokic and Strugar both at the time of the events, that is on the 6th and 7th of December when there was some apologies made to the Croatian side, and also tries to compare the statements they each made at their respective hearings and they argue basically, look, they're very similar in content. This technique, this parsing or this hyper-textual examination of their words misses the main point, the main point of difference. Unlike Strugar's words, Jokic's words at trial and at the time were fully backed up by objective evidence of his remorse, his plea of guilt, and his substantial cooperation. And General Strugar cannot claim either of those. The Defence has highlighted in their briefs the Vasiljevic Appeals Judgement which affirms that it is possible for an accused to express sincere regrets without admitting his participation in a crime. In other words, that going to trial doesn't preclude an accused from demonstrating sincere remorse. Remorse doesn't require an admission of criminal guilt. This may very well be true. But this doesn't mean that an accused who elects to go to trial can always get the benefit of the mitigating factor of remorse. Now, the accused, of course, has the right to plead not guilty. He has the right to fully defend the charges against him or her. However, there may be consequences of strategies pursued at trial such as running a full defence on crime base, on responsibility, on links, there may be consequences of putting forward a series of alternative defences as was done in this case, and one of those consequences may be that the accused simply is no longer able to avail himself of remorse as a mitigating factor. The Vasiljevic Appeals Judgement stands for the proposition that going to trial is not necessarily inconsistent with expressing remorse, but it does not mean that all accused persons who are left to go to trial have the right to claim remorse as a mitigating factor, and nor that every -- each and every general statement of sorrow will necessitate a sentencing reduction. In our submission, more is needed than simply a broad apology without even admitting that crimes occurred, let alone any personal responsibility. This is for the reason -- this is for the reason that these types of statements do not serve any of the purposes or goals of -- any of the purposes or goals in sentencing which remorse seeks to achieve in the context of an international Tribunal, that is reconciliation, affirmative prevention and rehabilitation. We ask you to increase the sentence to more appropriately reflect his culpability. In terms of a concrete figure, at trial the Prosecution asked for a range of 13 to 15 years. Based on the convictions as found by the Trial Chamber, and bearing in mind Jokic's sentence, in our submission, an appropriate sentence by the Trial Chamber should have been in the range of 10 to 12 years and not 8 years. The last point I wish to address is the Defence's submission that asked you to consider Strugar's present health situation, what they say is the deteriorated health situation since his trial and sentence, since the judgement came out three years ago. We've already said the Trial Chamber already considered Mr. Strugar's poor health situation at the time of his trial and for the purposes of his sentencing and there's no error in the exercise of its discretion in having considered that factor. So in fact, I'm confining my remarks purely to Mr. Strugar's health insofar as it may have deteriorated since that time. In our submission, if Your Honours reach the point where you resentence General Strugar, either because you uphold our first ground of appeal and thereby widen the scope of his conviction, or because you find error and you uphold either sentence appeal, either the Defence's or the Prosecution's appeal against sentence on the basis that the Trial Chamber erred, then our answer would be yes, in the exercise of your discretion, you may consider evidence that the accused's health has significantly worsened since trial. And I say this on the basis of the Celebici Sentencing Appeals Judgement on the 3rd of April, 2003, paragraphs 11 to 15 which would allow that. However, in our submission, this would call for a careful exercise of your discretion. In the past, when you've been confronted by evidence on appeal of an accused's changed personal circumstances since trial, more often than not, you have not allowed in such evidence in the exercise of your discretion. For example, in the Zoran Zigic case when he tried to put forward further evidence on appeal of his post-sentence behaviour in the UNDU, and also in the Celebici Appeals Judgement itself, the Appeals Chamber also did not accept evidence of this changed circumstances. However, throughout these appeal proceedings over the past three years, I think it would be fair to say that both parties and the Appeals Chamber have been cognizant of the special health aspects of General Strugar's case. Mr. Rodic mentioned reports that have been filed over the past few years in 2004, I believe, 2005, 2006. So if you come to the stage where you're determining a new sentence for General Strugar, you may decide that this is such a case to exercise your discretion and consider his present state of health. We know about the reports that have been put forward by the Defence. So long as that evidence were capable of showing to Your Honours' satisfaction that there had been a deterioration in his health, it would not be an inappropriate exercise of your discretion, in our submission, to take those into account. That concludes my -- the Prosecution's submissions on sentence as well as the Prosecution's appeal. So unless there are any questions, that concludes from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question, Ms. Brady. You have cited the Vasiljevic case in support of the proposition that a defendant need not admit to the crimes alleged against him, whether he can, without making that admission, claim mitigation. Now, you said more is needed than a broad apology without admitting that crimes occurred. Now, if you were Defence counsel advising your client, you would want to know what more is needed than a broad apology if it is the case that he need not admit that any crimes occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Vasiljevic judgement actually says that an accused -- it is possible for an accused to express sincere regrets without admitting his participation in a crime. In our submission, what would need to be done at a minimum, and I believe this is where, in the past, Trial Chambers and Appeals Chambers have allowed or affirmed statements made as remorse in this situation where the person at least admits that some wrongdoing, some crime or wrongdoing was perpetrated. He can still, of course, run his Defence and -- run the defence that he himself bears no responsibility. His participation is nil, if that's his defence, but at some level, that some wrongdoing, some crimes occurred. For example, in the Musema case where there was no admission by the accused that he had participated or had responsibility for what had occurred in the genocide, however, he admitted that genocide had occurred. So at some level there has to be an acknowledgment of that wrongdoing or a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Brady. You have finished your presentation, have you? Very well. Thank you. Mr. Rodic, you have the floor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I could just ask you to allow me three minutes in the context of my previous question to respond to what Prosecutor Brady said in response to the Judge's questions and then my colleague will take over. Just two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My learned friend mentioned responding to the question posed by Honourable Judge Meron referring to transcript page 4086 to 4087 that upon return from Belgrade, Admiral Jokic allegedly spoke to General Strugar about the way to cover up events in the Old Town and events related to the shelling of the Old Town. I must say that such statements are not contained in the judgement, in the trial judgement, because the Trial Chamber did not accept that. Jokic, who was desperately fighting for a better position and a milder sentence at the time when he was testifying in the Strugar case gave evidence that was, like in many other cases, full of different versions and contradictions. His evidence is an attempt to present a version to the Croatian public and there is no corroborating evidence that would confirm such claims made by Jokic. Therefore, the Trial Chamber completely ignored this part of Jokic's testimony. The issue was the punishment for Kovacevic and why Jokic did not punish him. If we look at the consequences of the investigation and the taking of various steps, and if we take that it is very important as it is important to us, to determine the conduct of Jokic on the 5th of December, if Jokic was planning with Kovacevic and giving orders to Kovacevic without the knowledge of the 2nd Operations Group, then the involvement of Kovacevic is much greater and the blame is laid -- and left Colonel Jovanovic who ended up punished. Jovanovic who, as the Trial Chamber established, was not able to use his artillery against the Old Town. In response to the Judge's questions, my learned friend said that at 7.00 in the morning, Strugar was informed by Kadijevic that the Old Town had been shelled and then he proceeded to call Jokic; however, this is a misinterpretation. At that moment, Kadijevic could not have known anything about the Old Town and thus Strugar was unable to know and he could not intervene in the area of Dubrovnik. The Trial Chamber also accepted that in its judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to respond to the appeals of the Prosecution. This is the response of the Defence to the Prosecution's appeals brief and the arguments presented today. These arguments are very similar to the written filings of the Prosecution. To these written filings, the Defence has responded in detail, and the Defence stands by its reply to the Prosecution's appeal. We do wish to highlight certain points that we feel could be useful to the Appeals Chamber in making its decision. The first appeals ground of the Prosecution regards the obligation of the accused to prevent crimes by his subordinates in keeping with Article 7(3). The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Strugar did not know or had reason to know that his subordinates would commit a crime during the attack on Srdj and this concerns the attack on Srdj of the 6th December, 1991, which, in the finding of the Trial Chamber was ordered by Strugar. The Prosecutor argues that Strugar had the obligation to take steps to prevent the Old Town from being shelled during that attack and he had this obligation from the moment on the 5th of December when he ordered the attack, that is, from 0000 hours on the 6th of December, 1991, bearing in mind the time frame set by the indictment. This ground of appeal rests on the assumption which underlies the very trial judgement. The underlying premise in the trial judgement, namely that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December, 1991. First and foremost, the Defence emphatically rejects the proposition that Strugar ordered the attack on Srdj as stated in the judgement. The Appeals Chamber has already had occasion to hear our arguments on this subject. In this response to the Prosecution, the Defence will not repeat any of the arguments regarding the error in fact made by the Trial Chamber in the finding that Strugar gave the order to attack. All this is contained in the response by the Defence. This ground of appeal of the Prosecution obtains if, and only if the Appeals Chamber does not accept the key ground of appeal of the Defence. If the Appeals Chamber takes the position that there was no order, the Defence believes that it is superfluous to discuss the scope of his obligation to prevent acts referred to in this ground of appeal of the Prosecution. If, however, the Appeals Chamber rejects the appeal of the Defence in this segment, then the Defence would wish to highlight certain reasons which, as we believe, justify the position of the Trial Chamber in this part. The Defence understands that the Prosecution draws from the legal reasoning of the Trial Chamber the conclusion that the Trial Chamber sees the responsibility of the superior only when a crime is certain, for instance, when it is preplanned. In other situations, in the interpretation of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber does not imply the superior's obligation to act. In fact, the Prosecution erroneously concludes that the Trial Chamber requires as a condition for a superior's responsibility that the superior knows or has reason to know only if there is certainty that the crime will occur. This conclusion of the Prosecution is inaccurate. It is our assertion that the Trial Chamber does not deviate from the accepted interpretation of requirements for responsibility under Article 7(3). On the contrary, the finding of the Trial Chamber is a result of a careful evaluation made by the Trial Chamber, namely of the circumstances whether the superior knew or had reason to know. This evaluation also covers real and obvious risk. This evaluation is made regardless of the issue of existence or non-existence of a plan of attack or plan to commit crimes. In this careful evaluation, the Trial Chamber took into account all the factors and reviewed them thoroughly. The factors taken into account by the Trial Chamber are enumerated in paragraphs 32 and 33 of the Defence response brief. All these facts are evaluated by the Trial Chamber in the context of the existence of a real and obvious risk that the JNA would shell the Old Town in the course of executing the action on Srdj. All these facts that the Chamber analyses are a risk evaluation, that is an evaluation of whether the accused in this context knew about that risk or had reason to know. The Chamber evaluates the risk, it does not look for certainty that a crime will occur, and it does not look for a plan that would imply Strugar's obligation to act. In this evaluation of risk, the Chamber only quotes as an example a situation that the -- where the superior had information that forces under his control were planning to commit a crime. The Chamber uses this as an example, not a condition, not a requirement. The Prosecutor, in fact, disagrees with the results of the factual risk evaluation, not with the legal position of the Trial Chamber. It seems that the Prosecution takes as a standard for Article 7(3) in such a way that the superior would have notice of risk in every case when he has information that certain subordinates had committed certain crimes earlier. The Defence is under the impression that the approach of the Prosecution implies an automatic formula. And the Defence believes that instead, on this point, an evaluation has to be made as well, particularly because in relation to events in October and November 1991, there is a whole series of factually contestable issues, what crimes were involved, who committed the crimes, where it was established that events from October and November could be characterised as crimes, and especially whether these crimes had the same elements as the crimes that occurred on the 6th December 1991. It is also very important who committed these alleged crimes. In relation to the shelling of October 1991, the evidence led clearly indicates that it was not the unit that Strugar allegedly ordered to take Srdj on the 6th of December 1991; the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade did not participate in activities in October 1991. In the evidence of the case, there are exhibits in evidence where this unit was at that time and it was in no way involved in attacks on Dubrovnik or the Old Town. This was dealt with in detail in paragraph 13 of the Defence brief. Concerning events in November 1991, artillery support was provided by ships from the sea and other artillery units of the 9th Military Naval Sector, so again it was not artillery fire opened by the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. This can be found in paragraphs 19 through 28 of the Defence appeals brief. Thus, even if we accept the position of the Trial Chamber regarding the alleged order to take Srdj, the very fact or the mere fact that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade was engaged does not mean that the accused had reason to know or could have known that in view of their earlier conduct, there was a risk of an attack on the Old Town occurring again. So this automatic formula used by the Prosecutor to show that notice of risk exists always whenever there is information of earlier crimes is completely inconsistent with the case law of this Tribunal to which the Defence refers in its Defence response brief. The position of the Appeals Chamber in the Krnojelac case, paragraph 171 of that judgement is completely consistent with the approach demonstrated by the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case. As stated earlier, the Trial Chamber evaluated a whole set of circumstances in making its finding on whether the risk that existed in executing the alleged order to take -- or to attack Srdj was such that Strugar could have known or had reason to know. To conclude, the Defence believes that the Trial Chamber did not make an error in law in applying the legal standard to the evaluation of whether Strugar knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit a crime. In response to the second ground of appeal that was not mentioned by the Prosecution today, we are not going to respond except to say that our arguments are already stated in our Defence response brief. Therefore, I shall move on to the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution, errors in sentencing. I will now address the third ground of appeal of the Prosecution, the errors in sentencing. The Prosecutor claims in her third ground of appeal that when determining a sentence for Strugar, the Trial Chamber attempted to compare the situation of Jokic to that of Strugar. The Prosecutor also submits that the Trial Chamber made an erroneous evaluation of the respective roles of Jokic and Strugar in what happened at the time by stating that Strugar was more remote from what was going on than Jokic, or more remotely responsible. They also appealed the fact that Strugar got only one year more than Jokic in terms of a sentence although there are significant mitigating circumstances in Jokic's case in relation to Strugar. One thing that I don't think that will be challenged by anyone in this courtroom that sentencing must be strictly individualised and that the sentencing of Strugar was a highly sensitive procedure taking into account a whole number of factors starting with the gravity of the crime itself and Strugar's role ranging all the way to a whole number of mitigating circumstances that have been established in Strugar's case. Starting from this basic premise, the Defence wishes to point out the key differences between Jokic's case and Strugar's case and we also wish to present our understanding of the allegations in the judgement that the Prosecution addresses in terms of Strugar being more remotely responsible than Admiral Jokic and, therefore, less responsible on the whole. When determining a sentence, the key factor is the gravity of the crime and the gravity of an accused's overall culpability. Culpability -- the culpability of an accused is reflected through the crimes for which an accused is convicted. The Trial Chamber found Jokic guilty of six crimes charged under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Strugar was acquitted of all charges under 7(1). When sentencing Strugar, the Trial Chamber dismissed everything under Article 7(3) in relation to Jokic. Jokic was convicted in relation to six crimes and Strugar in relation to two. The severity of the sentence imposed is in direct relation to the gravity of the overall criminal conduct. The crimes and forms of criminal responsibility for which Jokic was convicted are difficult to compare to the crimes for which Strugar was convicted and this difference is reflected in the sentence eventually imposed. It is entirely erroneous of the Prosecutor to claim that Jokic and Strugar were charged with the same crimes. This is an erroneous interpretation of facts as we see them. In addition to that, the Trial Chamber imposed on Jokic a sentence bearing in mind the scope of destruction that he was found guilty of. Jokic was convicted for destroying no less than 450 buildings in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Strugar, on the other hand, was convicted only in relation to the destruction of 52 buildings, a figure arrived at by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber convicted Jokic for cruel treatment and attacks on civilians in relation to two persons who were wounded on the 6th of December, 1991. Strugar was only convicted in relation to two persons in terms of attacks against civilians. The Trial Chamber also found an aggravating circumstance in relation to Jokic, however, no aggravating circumstances were found in relation to Strugar. Another thing that the Defence would like to emphasise is the opportunity enjoyed by the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case to directly inspect the role of Jokic even to a far greater degree than the Trial Chamber that eventually convicted Jokic himself. Jokic spent over a month testifying in this trial. The Defence is convinced that the disparity in sentences that now exists and which the Defence believes to be inadequate and to be at Strugar's expense, and this is something that we deal with in our appellate brief, is precisely a result of the Chamber's assessment in the Strugar case of Jokic's role in the events after the events of the way Jokic described these events and of the way Jokic gave evidence before the Trial Chamber. The sentence itself is a result of this overall assessment. Paragraph 464 of the judgement says that Strugar was not as directly responsible as Jokic. The Prosecutor draws the impossible inference that the Trial Chamber finds him to be less responsible because he was Jokic's superior and was above him in the actual chain of command. The Trial Chamber finds that Strugar is more remotely responsible because such are the facts of the case because that is what the evidence points to. The Prosecutor submits that Strugar had a high level of effective control as opposed to Jokic and this fact alone justifies the disparity in sentences between the two. The Defence is of the opposite opinion. The level of control that Jokic had was far higher and far more comprehensive than the one that Strugar had. In this context there are a number of conclusions and findings by the Trial Chamber that the sentence itself is based on. The Defence would like to point out a number of conclusions which we believe to be consistent with the facts as they are. This is in relation to Jokic's role in these events. These are a mere handful of conclusions that I will be raising now. Other conclusions were raised in other places and there is no need to go into that again. All the forces involved in the attack were under Jokic's direct command; and this is something that was determined by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber further established that Jokic was the logical choice, if not the only choice, in terms of who would have been in charge of an investigation. The Chamber concludes that Jokic was the only logical choice and this strays or deviates in no way from the doctrine used by the JNA or from the principles of command that prevailed in the JNA. This same Jokic was quite adamant when he answered this question that Strugar never, including the 6th of December, 1991, ordered any attack on the Old Town or Dubrovnik, generally speaking. Jokic admitted his own guilt probably because he was directly responsible to what was going on around Dubrovnik in the Old Town since this was his own area of responsibility and his own units were in charge in the area. Jokic used this opportunity in the absence of evidence led by the OTP and that is why his admission was a limited one. However, during the Strugar trial itself, a lot of light was shed on Jokic's involvement in events of the 6th of December, 1991, which appears to have been far more serious than that defined in Jokic's admission of guilt. Now, the Prosecutor drops charges that they have previously levelled at Warship-Captain Zec. They have Jokic's limited admission and, while no valid evidence is being adduced, they want to make up for this in terms of heightening Strugar's responsibility for what happened on the 6th of December, 1991. Their conclusion on Jokic's role is this, Jokic had direct and effective control over the units. His responsibilities and duties in terms of preventing and punishing the developed events that took place on the 6th of December were in Jokic's hands. Not only is there a discrepancy in sentences between Jokic and Strugar - this should be done at Strugar's expense - the Prosecution claims but the Defence claims that exactly the opposite should be the case and we have detailed this request and proposal in our brief. As to Strugar's statement, the first thing I would like to point out is this: The Defence submits that the issue of the importance or weight attached by the Trial Chamber to Strugar's sentence, the weight given his statement is insignificant and this precisely is one of the arguments that the Defence wishes to adduce. We believe that the Trial Chamber did not give sufficient weight to this statement, that it did not give this statement the weight that merited. The Defence thus remains somewhat in the dark as to why the Prosecutor would be objecting to anything in relation to Strugar's statement. It was merely mentioned in the statement of reasons of the trial judgement but it was not afforded any major weight at all. The Chamber never actually establishes whether they took the statement into account as a mitigating circumstance or not and if so, to what extent. The Defence is inclined to conclude that no weight whatsoever was given to the statement made by Mr. Strugar and certainly not the weight that it would have deserved. Should the Appeals Chamber find that there was weight that was given to this statement, I would say that this must be based on the positions expressed by the Appeals Chamber and as explained by the Appeals Chamber today in relation to the position expressed in the Vasiljevic case. Therefore, nowhere in that paragraph of the Appeals Chamber do we find any reference to conditionally accepting any form of admission or responsibility for what is at stake in a trial as a whole. The Prosecutor claims that a single year of difference between the two sentences is simply inadequate. They seek that the expressions of remorse of Strugar and Jokic respectively be identified and that Strugar's sentence be heightened. We wish to point out that there is a whole number of factors that affect this situation: Personal situations of the two accused, their respective health and a whole number of other circumstances that affect the obvious differences between the two cases. The Defence would particularly like to point out the following: I'm talking about the allegations of the Prosecution saying that the difference in the sentence between Jokic and Strugar must reflect Jokic's substantial cooperation. The Defence believes that it is precisely this segment that can be best used to evaluate the difference between the sentence imposed on Strugar and that imposed by the Trial Chamber on Jokic. The Defence submits, as I said a while ago, that the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case had an excellent opportunity to see for themselves what this cooperation was about, what Jokic was trying to say, what Jokic was trying to conceal, what Jokic was trying to play down, and where Jokic was simply not telling the truth. The Trial Chamber properly assessed this cooperation on Jokic 's part in their judgement. Whenever key facts were concerned, the Trial Chamber refused to lend credence to what Jokic said. Although he was committed to cooperation, the real scope and success of his cooperation as part of achieving justice boils down to this: Jokic's attempt to minimise his own responsibility and to shift the blame to Strugar. We have addressed this issue before. Now we shall merely quote a number of findings of the Trial Chamber in relation to Jokic's evidence. Paragraph 881 of the judgement shows us that the Trial Chamber establishes how Jokic stated following negotiations on the 5th of December, 1991, that a single issue was -- remained unresolved, the control of ships. In paragraph 83, the Trial Chamber establishes that Jokic's version was exaggerated and was putting too generous a gloss on the state of the negotiations on the 5th of December. Paragraph 83 of the judgement states that on the 6th of December 1991, questions occurred which Jokic stated had been resolved on the 5th of December. The question of lifting Dubrovnik's blockade in exchange for evacuating members of Croatia's armed forces. This was a request made on the 6th of December, 1991, which Jokic chose to remain silent about and the Chamber duly noticed this and stated so. In paragraph 82, Jokic talks about what he did after meeting Croatia's ministers. He claims that he, Jokic, informed the Accused Strugar about this in Trebinje. The Chamber refuses to believe Jokic in terms of the substance of what he said about Strugar. Jokic claims that he was not present at the meeting in Kupari on the 5th of December. The Chamber refuses to believe him. The question remains unresolved. The Chamber refuses to believe Jokic among other things because in his interview to the Prosecutor in 2003, he explicitly stated that he had been present at the meeting. When talking about Jokic's report dated the 7th of December, 1991, the Chamber deems it to be a report that seeks to dilute or deceive. Jokic, in 2004, at this trial, claims that reports he'd drafted in 1991 were part of a conspiracy against him. The Chamber believes that his explanation was simply not probable or credible. The Chamber assesses Jokic's evidence in relation to key aspects of the conviction, the roles of Strugar and Kadijevic. The Trial Chamber is dissatisfied and refuses to accept Jokic's explanation. The Chamber refuses to accept Jokic's evidence in his key components in terms of the key events on the morning of the of 6th of December, 1991. Despite all these facts, despite all the facts that a Trial Chamber established, and that Jokic knew about them on the 6th of December 1991, at the time of the trial when allegedly he makes an open confession regarding his own involvement in these events, his explanation is still that he did not take any steps because he did not have sufficient proof. The Trial Chamber finds his explanation to not be convincing. Jokic enters into an agreement with the OTP but he takes up a commitment to provide information that is complete and truthful. The only chance to check the truthfulness and completeness of any information provided by Jokic was the Strugar trial itself. By dismissing Jokic's allegations in all key aspects of the explanation that he provides as to what happened on the 6th of December, 1991, the Trial Chamber provided an effective evaluation of the quality and degree of his substantial cooperation. Another thing that the Defence wishes to point out in particular is the fact that the Prosecutor does not challenge Strugar's sentence, the severity of Strugar's sentence from the point of view of legal practice that prevails in the working international Tribunals. They never claim that the sentence was not properly determined because it was not in keeping with the criteria and requirements adopted by the international Tribunal. The height of the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber against Strugar can only be challenged from a point of view of legal practice but certainly not by comparing it to the sentence imposed on Jokic. A comparison between these two sentences is simply impossible and certainly not in the way that the OTP would like it to be. And especially if we take into account the gravity of the crimes involved and both mitigating and aggravating circumstances that were found. Any effect of aggravating or mitigating circumstances on a sentence must be individual and must depend on the case in hand. This is an approach allocated by the OTP in their third ground of appeal and it seems to neglect the individual circumstances regarding this particular accused. The Defence asked the Trial Chamber to dismiss this third ground of appeal of the OTP. And we also ask the Trial Chamber to dismiss the -- all the grounds of appeal of the OTP in their entirety. What I would finally like to do is this: I would like to briefly respond to the question of the Honourable Appeals Chamber with regard to the letter dated the 20th of March, 2008. The Defence believes, as far as an attack on civilian facilities is concerned, the same kind of mens rea is required as that required for an attack against civilians. The Defence would like to reiterate its position that we are here talking about direct intent. Although we have perhaps not been sufficiently clear about this, I would like to say that we address this issue in paragraph 71 of our appellate brief. Thank you very much, Your Honours. This is our response to the allegations raised by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to thank Mr. Petrovic. We shall now give the floor to Ms. Brady from the Prosecution, for the Prosecution's reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President and Your Honours. We can be very brief in our reply. I will make a few brief comments on some of the submissions made in response to our sentence appeal and Ms. Jarvis will make a few brief comments in relation to the first ground. The first point I will make in relation to the sentence appeal is that it is a sentence appeal brought on the basis that the sentence is manifestly inadequate. In our submission, the comparison with Mr. Jokic's sentence both caused or contributed to the error and it also exposes the error and it's simply a too lenient sentence. The second point I'd like to make is a very simple one just to correct my friend in his reference to the number of buildings that were encompassed by the scope of Mr. Jokic's plea. He referred to, I think, the figure of 450 buildings. Your Honours' attention is drawn -- I draw Your Honours' attention to paragraph 27 of the Jokic sentencing -- excuse me, the Jokic trial judgement, paragraph 27 in particular footnote 34 that refers in fact to a smaller figure of buildings damaged being 100 buildings, not 450. The final submission I would like to make in reply is in relation to the submission we've heard from Mr. Petrovic if I could summarize it this way: He made the submission that basically Jokic spent one month testifying before the Trial Chamber and the Trial Chamber would have had a particularly box seat or a good opportunity to assess their respective roles. And they make the submission that Jokic's involvement in the crimes on the 6th of December was more serious in the view of the Strugar Trial Chamber than defined in the Jokic's -- than defined in Jokic's admission of guilt and as found by the Jokic Trial Chamber. They also make the submission that the Trial Chamber would have had the best view, as it were, in assessing the "cooperation" by Jokic. In relation to that grouping of submissions, we say this: It's true that the Trial Chamber in Strugar may well have had the opportunity, of course it had many days of hearing Mr. Jokic's testimony. I think it has to be remembered, however, that the Strugar Trial Chamber was not making findings or determinations on Mr. Jokic's guilt, indeed that was not the exercise; it was the trial of Mr. Strugar that was in its consideration. However, we agree that to an extent, to a large extent, the Trial Chamber did make findings accepting or rejecting aspects of Jokic and his description of his role on that day. However, in our submission, to the extent that they did that, it does, in fact, fit precisely within the findings made by the Jokic Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber's findings in Jokic as affirmed by this Appeals Chamber, it fits within Jokic's responsibility being one of aiding and abetting for failing to prevent because from the early hours of the morning, Jokic was on notice that the crimes were going on and he failed to take adequate measures, reasonable and adequate measures to prevent or punish. So to the extent that my learned friend had alleged a difference, we say that there is none between these perspectives as it were of Jokic's criminality. There's no difference between Strugar Trial Chamber and how the Jokic Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber in that case saw Jokic. In any respect, in any event, if -- because the Trial Chamber was comparing the sentence, was looking at Jokic's sentence, seven years, as the mark, as a reference point, as a comparative reference point, to the extent there was some difference in how they would have seen his role, then it really was bound to take the view of Jokic's responsibility as found by the Jokic Sentencing Chamber and as affirmed now by the Appeals Chamber. Because otherwise, there would be no point in the exercise of the comparison. The comparison of seven years only makes sense, the seven-year figure has to be seen as being a figure which was a sentence appropriate for certain criminality and that certain criminality as defined by the Jokic Trial Chamber and affirmed by the Appeals Chamber is what is the -- should be governing in this situation and not necessarily the Trial Chamber's view of Jokic. But in any event, we say that their views are consistent and the Trial Chamber was within the -- was fully in conformity with the views of the Jokic Sentencing Chamber. That's all I wish to say on points on sentencing so I'll hand over now to Ms. Jarvis who will make a few remarks on the first ground. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just three points to make in reply in relation to the Prosecution's first ground of appeal. The first one concerns the argument the Defence have raised that the Prosecution's first ground of appeal is entirely dependent on the Chamber's finding that Strugar issued the order to attack Srdj. Your Honours, I would like to clarify that our position is that the Prosecution's first ground of appeal is not so dependent on that particular legal finding. Certainly, we have argued in our brief and I've continued that line of argument here before you today that the particular context of Strugar's order to attack Srdj on the 5th of December certainly heightened the risk that the shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik would occur; but, Your Honours, even if you remove that contextual factor from the mix, we say there are still sufficiently compelling factors to trigger Strugar's duty as a commander to prevent crimes at the earlier time. Your Honours, in particular, when I started my submissions, I gave you a list of some 10 factors, contextual factors which together were relevant in assessing the real and obvious risk known to Strugar. Of these, there were three that were relevant to the order to attack Srdj and these were, in particular, the fact that, for example, the order to attack Srdj inherently in it was the prospect of wider shelling in Dubrovnik, that kind of thing. But even if you remove this from the evidentiary mix, what you're left with is a situation where, at least -- at the very least, Strugar knew that there had been a repeated pattern of shelling of the Old Town of Dubrovnik in October and November, that nothing had been done to punish these crimes, that it was in keeping with the general state of lack of discipline within Strugar's troops and of unauthorised fire and the like, and that even the existence of previous orders prohibiting attacks on cultural property and the Old Town, in particular in the case of the November shelling, were totally ineffective. We say that in that kind of a scenario, there is still a sufficient risk of the repetition of future crimes to require a superior to take action. We draw support for that position from the case law I've mentioned, for example, the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber which yesterday confirmed that in particular, the failure to punish past crimes is very relevant to the risk assessment because of the encouraging effect, the impunity, the impression of impunity that it generates amongst forces. I would also mention to Your Honours the Naletelic Appeal Judgement, and this is cited in our supplementary filing last year, where the Appeals Chamber found contrary to the ground of appeal raised in that case that Naletelic's personal observation of even one instance of his subordinates looting was sufficient to put him on notice and obligate him to take action to punish the perpetrators and prevent further plunder. That's at paragraph 386 and 387. So although we acknowledge certainly that is it is a case-by-case assessment, we say that in the circumstances of this case, even absent the context of the order to attack Srdj, there is sufficiently alarming information to have required Strugar to prevent those crimes. My second point concerns the argument the Defence have raised that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade was not involved in the November shelling and therefore, Strugar couldn't have been expected to have predicted that they would engage in the December shelling. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's finding in this respect is set out in a number of different places of the judgement in similar terms, but what I will refer you to for present purposes is footnote 1222 of the judgement where the Trial Chamber bases its finding that Strugar knew, based on prior criminal conduct of the 3rd Battalion of the repetition of future crimes. The Trial Chamber relies on the evidence that Admiral Jokic gave at trial about the fact that he conducted an investigation into the November shelling of the Old Town which led him to specifically conclude that this brigade was in a position to have carried out the shelling and that he subsequently confirmed that Captain Kovacevic, the commander, was the primarily responsible person. He then testified that he had followed up with General Strugar requesting that various commanders of the 472nd Brigade should be removed. Your Honours, essentially what the Defence challenge is doing now is suggesting that you should take a different view of the evidence to that that the Trial Chamber, based on its careful assessment, came to at the conclusion of the case. He hasn't shown that the Trial Chamber's finding was unreasonable and to the contrary, the finding is actually very much supported by the evidence about how the attack in November unfolded. Your Honours, in particular, what I'd refer you to is the trial judgement at paragraph 64 which talks about the 12 November shelling of the Old Town by the so-called Maljutka rockets, the wire-guided missiles. And the Trial Chamber talks about over evidence before it in particular from Captain Nesic who was part of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade who was stationed at Zarkovica during the November attack and who testified that the Old Town was shelled using these wire-guided missiles. So this is entirely consistent with the conclusions that Jokic drew in his investigation about the involvement. The Defence argument that the 3rd Battalion could not have been involved in the shelling is based on a wrong premise. They claim by reference to certain orders in relation to the November attack that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade was being supported by other artillery and wasn't tasked with any artillery assignments itself and so therefore, it could not have been responsible for the shelling. Your Honours, as the evidence at trial established, for example, in the trial judgement at paragraph 127, the 3rd Battalion had its own artillery and as Jokic testified as well at trial, it was entirely within keeping with military doctrine for these subordinate brigades to use their own artillery without being specifically directed to do that by a higher force. So the fact that they were being supported by artillery doesn't in any way undermine the conclusion that they could have used their own artillery on the 12th of November to shell the Old Town. And as I've said, that's really consistent with the evidence of the way the November attack unfolded. Your Honours, my final point concerns the Defence argument that the Prosecution is really unhappy with the Trial Chamber's risk assessment. And I want to clarify our position on that because that really is the essence of it. It's not that we are unhappy with the Trial Chamber's risk assessment. To the contrary, what we are unhappy about is that having assessed that the risk was a real and obvious one of a future repetition of crimes, that the Trial Chamber then attributed no legal duty to Strugar to do anything about it. So at its core, our appeal accepts the Chamber's own finding on the level of risk involved but seeks to argue that different legal consequences flow from that assessment. Your Honours, if I can conclude by asking you to think about the matter in these terms: What we're talking about here is a question of allocation of risk. Who should bear this real and obvious risk of future crimes? The Trial Chamber's approach was to say that the civilian population of Dubrovnik of the Old Town of Dubrovnik should bear that risk. That sitting their defenceless within the walls of the Old Town with all the might of the JNA artillery poised above it, those civilians who were in no position to control the risk had to bear the risk that those crimes would subsequently recur. We say that's contrary to the notion of superior responsibility and the doctrine of responsible command, the fundamental duty of a commander to control his troops. We say that the risk should lay with General Strugar who was the commander, the senior commander of the operative forces in the area who had every means at his disposal to control that risk, ensure that the shelling of the Old Town never started but who simply failed to act. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Kwon has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, I just noted you submitted that -- at page 140, line 15 that your appeal accepts the Chamber's -- Trial Chamber's own finding on the level of risk involved. How would you read the paragraph 418, in the middle of that paragraph, the sentence to which footnote 1204 is attached? "His knowledge in the Chamber's finding was that only a limited number of such Croatian defensive positions could exist and that as the attack progressed, these positions could be subjected to controlled and limited JNA shelling targeted on these positions or on what were believed by his forces to such positions." "To be such positions."

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we say this doesn't change the nature of our complaint in this case, that what the Trial Chamber was doing here was perhaps harking back to a finding it had made earlier about whether Strugar's duty -- Strugar's liability could be characterised as ordering based on his order to attack Srdj and whether that attached with it the awareness of a substantial likelihood that in the course of the attack, the Old Town would be unlawfully shelled. One of the reasons that the Chamber gave for ruling out a substantial likelihood was precisely because it considered that Strugar had ordered a more confined and controlled attack. But Your Honours, that doesn't undermine the other specific findings in the judgement in paragraphs 416, 417 and then again at paragraph 420 where the Chamber notwithstanding that analysis finds that he knew of a real risk that in the heat of the attack on Srdj, the JNA artillery would repeat its recent and already repeated conduct of the unlawful shelling on Dubrovnik. The problem is that at that juncture, they find that's not a sufficiently high level of risk and that's the point of our appeal is we say that must be -- that a superior in a position where he knows of not just a general possibility of crimes, not just a slight or remote risk, but a real risk, a present -- a recent -- based on recent past conduct and all the other factors, that a commander in that situation should be required to act precisely because he is the one who is in control of the lethal force that is putting at risk civilians and civilian objects in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Jarvis. I believe that Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a short question. I only ask this question by way of seeking information. As to what is the reference in the trial judgement to the proposition that the Trial Chamber found that it was for the civilians in Dubrovnik to bear the risk, unless I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm not suggesting there was such a finding in the judgement, not an express reference to that. My point was that that was the effect of what the Trial Chamber had done in this case. So I apologise if that wasn't clear from my earlier submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I believe that there aren't any more questions. I'm now going to turn to Mr. Strugar and ask him whether he wants to make a statement. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I would like to address the Chamber. Your Honours, I am grateful to the Chamber for having given me this opportunity to address the Court directly during this Appeals Hearing. It is the end of the day almost, and my fate is being resolved before this International Tribunal. As I thought about what it was that I could state on this occasion, bearing in mind the appeal filed and the oral arguments presented by my lawyers, I decided to highlight a few questions only. When I was informed by the government of Montenegro that The Hague Tribunal had provided information to the effect that I had been charged with crimes on account of the crimes that were committed in Dubrovnik, I immediately responded that I would voluntarily appear before the Court, as soon as possible at that. I made that decision although at that time, in October 2001, I was in hospital because I had a kidney problem and it was the fifth time I underwent surgery. Nevertheless, I left the hospital and I went to The Hague on the 21st of October, 2001. Seriously ill, not having healed properly, I arrived in The Hague where the deterioration of my health continued. I met with the understanding of the Trial Chamber that made it possible for me to be provisionally released in order to continue my medical treatment in Podgorica. I was tried here for crimes related to Dubrovnik in 1991. I support everything that was written in my appeal regarding the judgement and everything that my lawyers said before you here today. I am expressing myself in the imperative. I did not order the attack on Srdj and I think that there is ample evidence showing that and that you will agree with this statement. I never said to Colm Doyle that I had ordered fire to be opened on Dubrovnik. Unfortunately, today we know that the main protagonist of these events was a sick man, retired Major Kovacevic. On the basis of a decision made by this Court was sent from the detention unit here to undergo medical treatment at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. This year, he was declared permanently unfit to stand trial and was therefore released from custody. I know of the suffering of people in Dubrovnik and I deeply regret that. I feel sorry for every person who was a victim in Dubrovnik. I feel sorry about all the damage caused to the ancient city. I'm also aware of the suffering of the families of my soldiers who had lost their lives. I, as a soldier, know what war is and I do not want that ever to be repeated again. Your Honours, please understand my suffering as well. What hurts me the most is that I have been accused of having issued an order that I never issued, in actual fact. I kindly ask the Chamber to understand that in a few months, I will turn 75, that I'm an old and sick man. I had kidney surgery five times. I have prostate problems, I also have an artificial hip. The doctors say that I should get another artificial hip. They say that I should have surgery on both knees. My wife is very seriously ill and therefore, she hasn't visited me in years. When pointing this out, I am not asking for you to feel sorry for me. I just wish that you understand the position that I am in. Your Honours, I am sure that you will carefully analyse everything that was said here today and that you will reach a just and fair decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Strugar. Please be seated. I now wish to thank the Defence counsel and the Prosecution, the registry, the legal officers, the court reporters for their precious help, and the interpreters who made it possible for us to have these proceedings. We are now going to deliberate. You will be informed of the date of the Appeal Judgement in due time. The hearing stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.55 p.m.
